The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Raymond Prdfontaine) moved the third reading of the Bill (No. 201) respecting the; pilotage district of Montreal and the port and pilotage district of Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, before this Bill is read the third time I would like to ask my hon, friend (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) if he still persists in taking from the pilots of Quebec the Saguenay river ? I am sorry that I was not here when the Bill came up for its second reading or when the Bill was referred to the committee. If I had been I would have moved that the clause of the Bill which takes the River Saguenay from the pilots for Quebec and below, be erased from the BUI. I cannot see how my hon. friend is .going to make the Bill workable, because, as everybody knows, the pilots for the harbour of Quebec and below start their work at Bic in the county of Rimouski. Is it the object of the Bill, for instance to have one pilot to take a ship that is coming from Chicoutimi in the Saguenay river down to the mouth of the Saguenay, and then have another pilot take it from the Saguenay river to Bic ? The pilots will require to
have a station at the mouth of the Saguenay if the assumption that I have just referred to is right. If not then the pilot who tabes the ship from Chicoutimi or any other point in the Saguenay river down to Bic will have to be acquainted not only with the River Saguenay, but also with the part of the St. Lawrence river from the mouth of the Saguenay down to Bic. It seems to me that the plan proposed by the pilots is a sensible one and one which should have been adopted .by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, namely, that pilots, if they are found not qualified now to navigate the River Saguenay, should be given a chance to qualify themselves ; but, as far as my information goes, the pilots without any exception are perfectly qualified to navigate the Saguenay river. It is true that this summer one accident has taken place at the mouth of the River Saguenay. But this as far as my information goes, is the only accident that has taken place in a considerable number of years that is attributable to the pilot. The accident which occurred to the steamer ' Carolina ' could not be attributed to the pilots, because the pilots had nothing to do with it, but the accident which took place at the mouth of the Saguenay river is the only one that has occurred in a number of years that can be attributed to the pilot. In this case it was certainly an act of negligence on the part of the pilot. Under these circumstances I really believe that the hon. minister should drop that part of the Bill which relates to the Saguenay river. As has been pointed out by the pilots in their memorial which was read by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) the remuneration which they get is being reduced every year. Some time ago a decision was rendered in the vice-admiralty court in Quebec which was confirmed by the Exchequer Court by which barges in tow are not obliged to take pilots. This, of course, has also decreased the money earned by the pilots. Now, by taking away from the" pilots the Saguenay river-
We do not intend 1o take away from the pilots of Quebec the pilotage in the Saguenay river. The intention is simply to regulate the pilots and to see that they are duly qualified.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I cannot understand when my hon. friend says he does not intend to take away from the pilots of Quebec the pilotage of the Saguenay river, but that he only intends to regulate them, how he is going to carry out that intention. I cannot understand how he is going to regulate the pilotage on the Saguenay rivex-, apart from the pilotage between Quebec and Bic. Is he going to have one authority sitting in Ottawa, directiixg the pilots navigating the Saguenay, and another authority dii'ecting the pilots who navigate from Quebec down to Bic ? I call the attention of the minister to these facts, because I do not

think that the Bill, as presented to the House, can be made workable.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, before this Bill is read for the third time, I wish to lay before the House a memorandum submitted to the Quebec Harbour Commissioners, and to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries to its contents. That memorandum is dated Quebec, September 10, 1903, and reads as follows :-
Quebec, September 10, 1903. James Woods, Esq.,
Secretary-Treasurer of the Harbour Commissioners,
Quebec.
Dear Sir,-At a meeting of the Board of directors of Pilots, held yesterday, the letter from the deputy minister of Marine and Fisheries, dated 24th ultimo, was duly considered, and I hasten to acquaint you with the conclusion arrived at by my colleagues and myself
In the first place, the right of the pilots, granted by law, to act in the river Saguenay is recognized.
Inquiry is made as to whether the pilots object to the Marine Department assuming control.
In answer to that question, it is a matter of serious doubt whether the shippers, agents< consignees, &c., would gain much by having to deal with a government, whoever they may be, in order to obtain, even in a general way, a thoroughly efficient pilotage service. In our humble opinion, the pilots should under no circumstances be the creatures of a government. What is required primarily from the sailor is a thorough knowledge of his craft, such as will render him altogether reliable. Now, where are these competent men to be found ? We hear it stated over and over again that the unlicensed pilots of the firm of Price & Co. have not met with serious accidents in the river Saguenay. That may be true ; but we should not lose sight of the fact that these men have had to pilot only sailing ^vessels drawn by a tug, the 'Thor,' under the command of an experienced sailor. Now, the trade on the Saguenay river is carried on mainly by steamboats. These unlicensed pilots, who have never been out at sea, who have never served as sailors, who cannot even use the compass, would not be of much use in any emergency, such as occurred in the case of the ' Mersey ' or the ' Carolina,' &c. The Price men who act without a license are not liable in case of any accident, and do not come under the control of your board. We have already prepared a tariff, which was approved by your board, but it was pigeonholed at Ottawa. The members of the board respectfully suggest that the Department of Marine should place at the entrance of the Saguenay licensed pilots, known for their long experience of that river. There are, to say the least, about fifteen who are well qualified. As only two or three are required for that service, it is a very easy matter to attain the desired end. We have the pilot Boulanger, who keeps the Saguenay station, and who has already twenty-five years' experience and practice on that river. His ability cannot be denied by any one, and he has been requested more than once to replace those connected with the firm of Price & Co. See copy of letter attached as proof of this.

I shall not read that letter, as it is not important.
Thus the corporation of pilots is prepared to enter into the following agreement : Two pilots, recognized as having a long experience on the river Saguenay, and whose ability nobody could deny, would have the exclusive charge of piloting vessels on that river. The licensed pilot Boulanger, who has already -a practice of twenty-five years on that river, would train the pilots in turn for some time, in order to qualify them thoroughly, and put them' in a position to replace later on those who would retire on account of old age or otherwise. The pilot Boulanger would, on board his yacht, survey the river from one end to the other, in all directions, with assistants, make soundings, and ascertain the best places for anchorage, &c.
No others but pilots appointed and salaried by the b<jard of directors would have a right to pilot, or have a charge of any vessel on the river Saguenay.
Some coalers have been taken away from the pilots : but the company, be it said in passing, have lost more than they have gained owing to the great waste of time ; as might be easily shown. The pilots are anxious to retain the rights they enjoy under the law, and are especially desirous of showing that they are in a position to fully meet, in all respects, the requirements of the shipping trade I remain, sir,
Yours very truly,

President of the Corporation of Pilots.
May I be allowed to draw the attention of the Minister of Marine, to the very wise suggestions contained in this memorandum. As this law is about to be passed, I wish the minister would defer its enforcement for some time in order to enable the pilots to put in practice what they suggest in this memorandum, and what will give to the trade and to the country as a whole all possible assurances as to safe navigation on the River Saguenay.	[DOT]
I hope that the hon. minister will consider my suggestions, which X submit in good faith, and though realizing the serious responsibility which rests on those who are entrusted with the safety of the travelling public on the rivers Saint Lawrence and Saguenay. But I must say that I would take exception to any discrimination being made as regards the River Saguenay, when the pilots are thus prepared to offer every guarantee with a view to ensuring public safety.

(Translation.) ' Mr. Speaker, the great majority of the pilots reside in the county of Portneuf, and for that reason, I take a particular Interest in the legislation which is now introduced by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I must say that I do not know of a class more worthy of consideration than that of the pilots. They are leading and influential citizens, who qualify themselves

by close application to carry on their work, and who, in the exercise of their functions, incur heavy responsibilities, since they are entrusted with the lives and property of individuals. When a pilot takes charge of a ship at Quebec or Montreal, he becomes responsible for the whole ship, for the lives of the passengers and crew, and for the rich cargo on board. It is obvious that a clear mind and great ability are required to lead safely ships of 10,000 tons, four or five hundred feet long through the channel, from Quebec to Montreal, a channel which is no where wide, and which, in places does not exceed 300 feet in breadth. It often occurs that the channel is only one or two feet deeper than the actual draught of the ship. So that the slightest sheering of the ship, the least mistake in steering, may bring about some fatal accident. Besides currents and winds are to be taken into account, and difficulties must be constantly overcome.
Mr. Speaker, if I make these observations on the life of the pilot, it is to show that all legislation relating to pilots and pilotage cannot be considered too seriously. The public should be protected by laws imposing on the pilots reasonable obligations ; and on the other hand, the pilots should be duly protected when it comes to pass judgment on their conduct and liability.
The pilots in the province of Quebec are divided into two classes : Those who take charge of ships on the lower Saint Lawrence from Quebec to Pointe-au-P6re, and those who do the same service between Quebec and Montreal. Those on the lower Saint Lawrence have long since secured the right of managing their own affairs, parliament having granted them an Act of incorporation.	?
The Bill under consideration refers to the pilots who are doing service between Quebec and Montreal. It is by far the most difficult part of the river. They have applied to parliament for an Act of incorporation, but that favour has been refused them. They have heretofore been under the control of the Montreal Harbour Commissioners, and it is easy to understand, Sir, why that system has not given full satisfaction. That body is apt to change often, and is made up of members who are not all conversant with the art of navigation, and who, consequently, are not all qualified to lay down safe rules for the settlement of difficulties which may arise between the pilots and the steamship companies. I may add that several of the commissioners are directors of companies whose interests in some cases come in conflict with those of the pilots.
I am glad to see the Department of Marine assume the control of pilotage and of pilots, for several reasons, and the principal is that the change has been advocated by the pilots themselves. However, I venture to suggest a change which I consider essential ; I think that two or three experienced pilots should be called upon to stay on duty, during the season of navigation, in the Department of Marine, here, in order to be in a position to supply the department with the necessary information and give them the benefit of their advice and their experience.
The government, in 1890, appointed a commission to inquire into matters relating to pilotage ; and in going over the report of that commission, I find, at page 8, that the commissioners take the ground that in all questions concerning the pilots, their duly selected representatives should be heard.
At page 9 of the same report, I read the following
As regards the grievances of pilots, set forth and detailed in the preceding pages, your commissioners beg to recommend the following :
The pilots are not judged by a competent tribunal.
We are of opinion that, proceedings against pilots on account of accidents happening to ships when navigating the waters covered by the pilotage between Montreal and Quebec, under the care of pilots, should be taken before a maritime court, made up of three experts, one of whom would be appointed by the harbour commissioners, another by the pilots (although it may not be necessarily a pilot doing actual service between Montreal and Quebec), and the third appointed by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. But if later on an admiralty court was established in Montreal, then such proceedings should be taken before that judge, with the assistance of two nautical assessors.
That report of the pilotage commission contains, Sir, a fair statement of the position of the pilots, and some suggestions, which, I hope, will be given effect to by the department of Marine and Fisheries.
I entertain the hope that the interests of the pilots will be safeguarded and that the public.will be benefited thereby.
Motion agreed to ; Bill read the third time, and passed.
The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Sir William Mulock) moved the third reading of Bill (No. 257) to amend the Civil Service Act.

Before this Bill is read a third time, there are one or two things to which I wish to call the attention of the House. Under the Bill, provision has been made for the promotion of, and increases of pay to certain clerks in the civil service; but other officials, namely. the officers of this House and certain others, have been singularly ignored. I wish to direct the attention of the Postmaster General to that fact.
For instance, the librarians of parliament, who are officers of parliament, who are not members of the civil service in the strict acceptation of the term, are to have their

case attended to, while other officials of this House have been ignored. I do not think this is right, and I wish to call the attention of the promoter of the Bill to the fact. Officers who take precedence of deputy heads are left at their present salary, which is considerably below the salaries of the other gentlemen to whom I have referred. The clerk of this House, the clerk of the Senate, the clerk of the Privy Council, take precedence of deputy heads of departments. I understand that some provision is being made for the clerk of the Privy Council ; his salary is being increased ; but the salary of the clerk of this House has not been increased, nor have the salaries of the other officials of this House. As I pointed out when the Bill was in committee, the salaries of the officials of this House are very much less than those of the officials of the Senate, gentlemen who do not perform one-quarter and in some instances not one-tenth of the duty performed by the officials of this House of Commons, * It seems to me that is a thing that should be remedied. If these gentlemen in the Senate are receiving too much, there should be some way of reducing their salaries. If they are receiving no more, and it is to be presumed that they are receiving no more than their services entitle them to receive, the honour and dignity of this House demands that its officials should be put on an equal footing with the officials of the other chamber. It seems to me that this is a matter of importance that ought to be considered, and that fair play and justice should be extended to all the officials in the service of the country. The same argument which the Postmaster General has used to justify an increase in the salaries of the officers who are affected by this Bill, can be used with equal force and effect in the case of the.officers to whom I have referred. The office of clerk of this House is a very important position. It is necessary that the incumbent of that office should be possessed of very high qualifications. There is no position on the bench of this country that requires higher qualification in its incumbent than the clerk of this House. I am glad, Mr. Speaker, to know that we have in the person of the gentleman who occupies that position today a worthy successor of the gentleman who so honourably and ably filled it in the past years. I .see no reason why the clerk of this House should not receive equal consideration with the deputy heads of departments. particularly when the onerous duties he has to fulfil are considered-duties which are in excess of those performed by gentlemen who have already received consideration at the hands of this government. In saying this I am speaking for myself ; I have had no consultation with any of my friends on this side of the House on this matter ; but I believe I am voicing the sentiments of the greater proportion of them when I say that we are desirous of having I

the officials of this House and the officials of the country generally paid reasonable and proper salaries. We do not believe in cheese paring along these lines. We think there is extravagance in the public expendi-dures, but we do not think there is any extravagance in properly paying the officials in the service of the country. We should have good officials, and we should pay them good salaries. I hope the Postmaster General will take these matters into consideration, and refer this Bill back and have it so amended as to include all these officers from the highest to the lowest. From the messengers up, there should be on increase of pay. Even the 'Hansard ' reporters should have an increase, this year at least, on account of the long session, which has been a great detriment to them.

I wish to draw the attention of the Postmaster General to an omission from the Bill of provision for the officers of the Militia Department who are not regarded as coming under the Superannuation Act or the Pension Act which applies to the militia. I do not know whether the minister's attention lias been drawn to the matter or not, but I think, he should give it his consideration. Will he kindly look into it, or has he looked into it ?

With reference to the point raised by my hon. friend from King's, New Brunswick, (Mr. Fowler), no doubt the government have to plead guilty of the charge of being careful of the finances of the country in regard to increases of salary. I understand that we are accused of cheese paring. It is not an altogether unpardonable offence, although perhaps it is unwise to underpay any person. However, in accordance with the character which is assigned to us of being extremely careful in the administration of the public funds, we must go slowly even in dealing with salaries, because the expenditure on salaries is a very large item. My hon. friend will find that there is a measure before parliament dealing with the salaries of the librarians. Perhaps his absence from parliament accounts for that oversight.

I have attended this parliament more than the hon. gentleman has ; and besides, I referred to what is proposed to be done for the librarians. The hon. gentleman must have been asleep, as he usually is when in this House.

With reference to the other point which the hon. gentleman raised, that this measure should embrace the employees of the two Houses, I may say that that question has been before this House and has been discussed ; and I have already said that the government do not wish to interfere with the privileges of the two Houses. It is their privilege, we understand, to regulate the salaries of their

officers, subject of course to the power, if the government choose to exercise it, of modifying or carrying out or not respecting their views. However, this is not a Bill dealing with the salaries of the officers of parliament; it is a Bill dealing with the salaries of those in the civil service. That is the reason that subject would not properly find a place in this Bill. As to the question raised by my hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes), that the Bill does not deal with the officers of the Militia Department, I would point out that the measure does not pretend to deal with the status or the salaries of all the officials of the government. It is less pretentious than that. It applies chiefly, almost exclusively, to those who are classified. There are some slight exceptions, as in the case of the outside service in the Customs and Inland Revenue Departments. The subject of the militia officers has not before been brought to the attention of the House, and it would be too late, I think, to reopen this question this session, if the measure now before the House awaiting its third reading is to become law this session. The subject is worthy of every consideration, and I have no doubt that my hon. friend having brought it to the attention of the House, it will in (j,ue time receive careful consideration.

I have listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for King's, New Brunswick (Mr. Fowler) with reference to the salaries of our public officials, and I cannot see why there should be any discrimination With reference to tlios'-e who by chance do not come under this Bill. I refer particularly now to the clerk of the House. It is delicate for me to offer a remark in reference to that gentleman, he being in the chair. I may say I have known him for a number of years and consider that he is a very worthy successor to his predecessor ; and in my opinion, although he does not come under the Civil Service Act, he and his staff should not be discriminated against as respects increase of salary but be given similar considerations as the others. I believe that my hon. friend the Postmaster General, who has charge of this Bill, has the same disposition as myself in this respect, and I hope that when the opportune time arrives he will look after the officials of this House and recognize their claims for services well rendered.

I concur in the remarks just made by my hon. friend and would like to have them apply to the assistant clerk of the House.
. Mr. WM. ROCHE (Halifax). I wish to endorse the remarks of the hon. member from Lunenburg'(Mr. Kaulbach). The clerk of our House is well known to us all. He lias been a member of parliament many years and is eminently well qualified to fill
the responsible position he now holds. I would therefore urge on my hon. friend the Postmaster General that, in increasing the salaries of other civil servants, we should not leave out of sight the clerk of the House. My acquaintance with our worthy clerk has extended over forty years, and my experience of him is that he has creditably tilled every position he has occupied and is most certainly, in his present position, the right man in the right place. He therefore should be treated as regards salary on an equality with other officials.

The other evening I drew attention to the fact that there were one or two classes in the outside service, concerning whom no provisions were made with regard to salary.
I pointed out that the preventive officers in the Customs and Inland Revenue branches were not provided for. In reply the Postmaster General referred me to subsection 2 of section 37, but that only provides for their appointment without examination. It does not stipulate what their salaries will be. It seems to me that they are as much entitled to an increase, according to length of service and faithfulness in the discharge of their duties, as any other class.
These are temporary officers not subject to examination, who can be removed at any moment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF INLAND REVENUE (Hon. M. E. Bernier).

speechtext: But they are usually kept on permanently.

These men may pass an examination and will then be subject for promotion, but at present they are not subject to any\ examination and they are not classified. I am simply following* the custom which has been in force for years.
I did not quite apprehend the reason given by my hon. friend the Postmaster General why the salaries of the officers of the House have not been taken into consideration ?

The Bill before the House is one dealing with the civil service and not with the officers of the House of Commons and the Senate. It is the privilege of these two Houses to deal with the salaries of their officers and employees, and the government does not desire to encroach on that privilege. It is open to this House, through its committee, to bring up the question of salaries in a report presented to the House, and if that report should be adopted, of course the government would give proper respect to the decision of the House. No such procedure has been adopted and the government do not feel warranted in taking from the House that ancient privilege. The government are extremely pleased to hear the expressions of opinion on all sides as to the

wisdom of the selection of the clerk of the House, which, I am positive, time will confirm. Although nothing is done on this occasion, the House will understand that the non-interference of the government is not to be regarded as in any way an indication that the government do not share the opinion of hon. members regarding the claims and merits of the gentleman selected for the high office of clerk of the House.

As the Civil Service Bill must be the subject of the attention of the government at an early date, I would like to point out that in the commonwealth of Australia the officers of both Houses of parliament have been placed under the Civil Service Act and are treated in the same way as the other permanent employees. The reason which has been advanced by the Postmaster General may be a good one, but 1 might point out to him a recent instance where, under conditions very similar to those which prevail in this country, it has not been considered a sufficient reason, and the contrary course has been adopted ; the clerks of both houses in the commonwealth of Australia have been put under the civil service list and treated in the same way as the rest of the officers of the commonwealth. I should think that that was a proper course and I cannot see why the officers of this House and of the Senate should be treated differently from the officers of any other department, under the control of either the House or the executive. The same reasons apply for putting the officers of the House or Senate under the permanent list, for providing them with superannuation and the other advantages of permanency in the service that apply to the different departments of the service. I hope when the matter is again under consideration that the precedent which I have cited may receive the attention and consideration of the government.

1 desire to emphasize the remarks of the hon. member for King's, N.B. (Mr. Fowler) as well as those of the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mnlock), and the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach), that the servants of this House are deserving of the same consideration as any other branch of the civil service of Canada. Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I desire to bring to the attention of the government and of the House a matter which affects a large portion of the population of the community in which I reside, and which

I have the honour of representing in this House. X have had the honour of bringing this question before the House on other occasions, but up to the present time nothing has been done in the matter. I refer to the claims of a great many settlers in the Saskatchewan district arising out of the rebellion of 1885. After the rebellion, the government of the day appointed a claims commission who were sent up to the Saskatchewan district with the idea of settling the claims of the settlers for losses incurred in that rebellion. The government of that day, apparently in a fair spirit, saw fit to appoint on that commission a resident of the district who was well known in that part of the country. The commission was appointed on August 25tli, 1885, and sat until January 6th, 1886, a period of 135 days. They brought in a report, which 1 have here, in which they recommended the payment of a certain number of claims. A Short time after that, as the election of 1887 was coming on in the near future, and as there was a great deal of dissatisfaction with reference to the unsettled claims, the government saw fit to send the same commission to settle the balance of these claims. On March 15th, 1886, this commission resumed its labours and apparently was employed until August 9th, 1887. During the summer of 1886, this commission took evidence in a great many cases and reserved (judgment as to what should be done in the matter of paying or not paying, and that is where the grievance comes in. One of these commissioners, a gentleman appointed from my district, came up to the Saskatchewan district in the fall previous to the election of 1887, and started to work as an agent in the interests of the government of the day. He attended public meetings and spoke at public meetings and worked among the people for nearly three months, until the election of March 15th, 1887.
Mr. 1,a RIVIERE. Would the hon. gentleman give the name ?

Mr. Thomas McKay, now a member of the local legislature. He spoke at these meetings and canvassed and worked there until the election took place. At * that time we had an open vote, and it was possible to know just how each elector voted. This gentleman, being in charge of the organization of the Conservative party in that district, was in a position to have access to the poll-books and everything of that kind and knew exactly how every man polled his vote at that election. When the election was over and the commission made its award, it was found that the gentlemen who had voted against the government of the day had received cold justice, while those who supported the government of the day were in some cases paid twice the amount that was legally due to them. The worst feature of the whole thing was-and I have the record under my hand-that during the three
months that Mr. McKay canvassed and worked and addressed public meetings in the interest of the Conservative party, he was receiving from the Dominion government $15 a day as claims commissioner and $5 a day for living expenses, and in addition his travelling expenses from here to Hie scene of rebellion and back again.
Now, I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is it possible that justice could be rendered to these people in a case of that kind ? Here was a paid official of the Dominion government who was getting $20 a day as claims commissioner going up and attending political meetings, and after he had attended the meetings, after these people had refused to vote as he wanted them to, this man is authorized to sit as a judge on their claims ? Could they expect justice in a case of that kind? They could not expect justice in a case of that kind ? They could not expect it, and they did not get it. These people have been agitating ever since, getting up petitions and sending letters, and they are not going to be satisfied until at least some steps are taken to investigate their grievance, and to see that the gross unfairness of the award of that commission has been rectified. Why, there are cases of men that we know of ourselves who were drawing $13,000 and $14,000 for losses of goods that one man could have carried on his back, while other men, bona fide settlers who did lose their all, got nothing or scarcely anything. I have all the reports here, the awards made, the amounts claimed, the amounts paid, and everything of that kind. I am not going into that, but I have briefly placed the facts before the House, and I would ask that some steps be taken to look into the mattter and see that these people get justice, because they certainly did not get justice at the hands of that commission; and every member on both sides of this House will agree with me that they could not expect to get justice from a gentleman who was paid $20 a day by the government for stumping up through Saskatchewan and who was afterwards sitting as a judge on the claims of these people.
It seems to me extraordinary that the hon. gentleman has sat in this House ever since he came here, and it is only at this late date that he brings this subject before parliament.
I want to draw attention to the fact that if the hon. gentleman goes through 'Hansard' he will find that I have brought the subject up several times in this House.

For several years there has not been a word from the hon. gentleman, but now he gets up, in the dying days of a long session, when it is expected there will be an election in the near future, and brings this subject to the attention of the

House, without notice of any kind. Now, whether this Mr. McKay did or did not act as a political agent during that time, it is impossible for us to say, at least it is impossible for me to say.

I have made a speech here in parliament showing that the people in my district know well whether he acted as election agent or not, and here is a return from the department which goes to show that he was paid for the time during which he was acting as agent. I think the proof is absolutely clear that he did.

The hon. gentleman, in my opinion, should have gone further, and he should have shown us from his records whether this gentleman did any work as a commissioner during that time, becanse if he had proven by the records which are in the possession of the department that he had not done any work at that time, then it might be assumed that he was acting only as a political agent, and was improperly paid for the time he was doing no work. But the hon. gentleman has not done that, and we are not in a position

Will the hon. gentleman allow me for a moment I make this statement, if he wants to know, that for two or three months after this gentleman was appointed claims commissioner he acted as political agent of the Conservative party in Saskatchewan, that he spoke from platforms, and he canvassed, and he did everything that an organizer had to do in Saskatchewan and he was paid $20 and travelling expenses by the government of the day while he was doing all that.
Did he sit as a commissioner ? Mr. DAVIS. Certainly not.
Then sit down.
Certainly he was not sitting on cases when he was electioneering.

Of course, we are obliged to accept the bon. gentleman's word, in the absence of any proof. I suspect, however, that if the records of the department were looked into it would be found that during the time the election campaign was going on he was acting as commissioner and not as a political agent, and doing his work as commissioner, and that from day to day.
I want to tell the hon. gentleman that he is absolutely wrong. He was not in the district and I was.

Then, it is a very strange fact that for several years, he has said nothing about it, although this must have been known by the hon. gentleman, because he says he brought it to the attention of the House after the last election in 1900. Now, we are in 1903, and there has not been a single word heard from the hon. gentle-

man since his own friends were in power. They had it in their power to give redress, if redress was required. Why did they not attend to this ? They have remained all this time perfectly oblivious to the injustice done to these people, until we are supposedly upon the eve of a general election, and then he gets up and makes this plea and shows that nothing has been done for these poor people. It seems to me, to use the language of the street, a little too thin. It looks more like an election dodge than anything else.
The hon. gentleman must not measure me from his own standpoint.

Well, I have seen so many efforts from that hon. gentleman along the same lines that I can now catch on to them pretty rapidly. They are well known. Now, with regard to these claims having been often discussed in this House, from my personal remembrance they have not been discussed frequently, and in my judgment, there never was a single instance where a good case was made out where the government were not disposed to do justice. But if justice was not done while his own friends have been in power for the last nine years, -and surely during that time
The time seems long to my hon. friend since he has been in opposition.

Well, nine years in the life of a government or in the life of a nation surely ought to be long enough to allow of these cases being brought to the attention of the government, and for them to do justice where injustice has been done. But the hon. member represented that constituency during all that time, and knew that injustice was done to these people-if his allegations be correct. Therefore, I say it is a strange fact that he has not secured justice for themi during all this time that his own friends have been in control. They have done -nothing but turn a deaf ear to his pleading ; so it does not seem to be exactly an appropriate time to bring it up now, but I suppose it answers the hon. gentleman's purpose.
Like provincial autonomy yesterday.

My bon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) is altogether astray in stating that my hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) has been tardy in bringing this question to the attention of the House and of the government. He has brought it more than once to the attention of the House, and he has brought it repeatedly to the atttention of the government. The circumstances with regard to these complaints are not new to me. I heard them when I was In opposition, and I have heard them since this government took office. The old government appointed a commission to

look into the losses which had been experienced by a good many residents in the North-west, and they made compensation for those losses. I know that some parties complained that they had not been fairly dealt with by the commission. These complaints were brought to me several times when I was sitting on the other side of the House, and they have been brought to my attention since this government was formed -repeatedly brought to my attention by the present member for the Saskatchewan district (Mr. Davis). It is always difficult, however, to re-open a matter of this kind after it has been closed for so many years, and the government did not see their way clear to have a further investigation into the mattter. The only thing I can say is that the government will look into the matter, but I will not pledge myself to anything more than that at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, the matter that has been brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis), as has been stated by the hon. member for Bast Grey (Mr. Sproule), would indicate the expectation of an approaching election. That is the view I would take of it. When we see the way in which that hon. gentleman has attacked a gentleman outside of this House, and when we observe the method he has used in order to injure a gentleman, who, I understand, is spoken of as very likely to be his opponent, we can readily understand why he has brought this question so forcibly to the attention of the House. The hon. gentleman has been a supporter of this government for seven years, and if he was not able to use his influence to do something for the people, who, he claims, have been so badly treated, I think this little speech that he has made in this House will not have a tendency to further their case to any great extent. I would not expect any hon. member of this House to attack a man who has no opportunity of defending himself. Anything may be said in this House under the cover of the privilege of the House against a man outside of it.
I made this attack upon the public platform. Mr. McKay could have come to my meeting, but he took the other road and never came.

The fact remains that if this gentleman has such a reputation as the hon. member for Saskatchewan would lead us to believe he is worthy of, it is a strange thing that he represents the people in the local assembly at Regina. Therefore, he cannot be so low in the estimation of his fellow citizens as the hon. gentleman would lend us to suppose he is. I can see pretty plainly what the intention of the hon. gentleman is, but if he is deceiving the people around Saskatchewan he is not deceiving 437
the people around this House. I have had some experience in supporting a government and I always found that if I could not induce the government by my own personal persuasions, with the assistance of my friends, to do a certain thing, I was very much less likely to do it by getting up and making a stump speech in this House. I would suggest to my hon. friend that he bring his persuasive powers to bear upon the government, that he surround himself with the members from the North-west Territories, Who are not backward in expressing their opinions, have an interview with the right hon. leader of the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and see if he cannot induce him to give a promise, and thus by his actions, which should speak much louder than his words in this House, show to the people of Saskatchewan that he is succeeding in doing something for their benefit, instead of getting tip and attacking a gentleman outside of this House who has no opportunity of defending himself.

Xj. BORDEN (Halifax). Mr. Speaker, I would suggest to my hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) that if he desires to have a matter of this kind intelligently discussed he should give some notice to the House, as I have no doubt he has given notice to the government, of his intention to bring it up. It is obvious that he could not have expected any very great benefit from the discussion, otherwise he would have adopted t he course that is usual. I do not know whether we have really gathered very much of importance from my hon. friend's remarks, except a suggestion that my hon. friend's presence on the platform terrified Mr. McKay so much as to deter him from going near him.

I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) is going a little astray in that statement. I was charged by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) with having attacked in this House a gentleman who did not have an opportunity of defending himself, and I stated that I had made the same attack on the platform, in the district where the parties were interested, and that Mr. McKay knew that I was going to do it, and that Mr. McKay did not turn up.
The hon. gentleman said that Mr. McKay immediately took the other road.
He was not there.

He was not only supposed to have run away from the meeting, but to have immediately taken the most rapid means of transportation in an opposite direction, so that he might not be within range of my hon. friend's eloquence.
He has been within range of it more than once.

I think he has not suffered from it. I am reminded of the fact that my hon. friend has sometimes had his suspectibilities wounded by attacks made upon gentlemen outside of this House. I think I have seen him displaying a great deal of feeling about references which have been made to officials of this government in the Yukon and elsewhere. But, in the remarks which my hon. friend has made to-day he seems to have entirely overlooked the considerations which influenced him at such times.
This gentleman is not an official; he is a public man.
He is a public man, but my hon. friend has made the deliberate charge against this gentleman

Which I am prepared to prove to this House.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax)-that he corruptly denied justice to these people. He said that being in receipt of some remuneration from the Conservative government, the people of the territory could not expect justice from him, and that they did not get it. This is a charge of a deliberate and corrupt denial of justice. Whether my hon. friend has proved it or not outside of this House it hardly seems to me to be a very courteous course to make the charge under the circumstances under which he has made it here. If there has been a corrupt denial of justice, it seems to me that it would have been the duty of this government upon coming into office, in 1896, to have investigated this matter, and I am surprised that my hon. friend, during the last seven years, has not brought it to the attention of the House in a more forcible way than he has to-day. There is no statute of limitations against a corrupt denial of justice, and if that has taken place it is a matter than should have been investigated long ago.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of supply.
Amount required for additional building at Banff. N.W.T., $10,000.

At the National Park at Banff, we have several buildings which have been in existence for some years and which enable visitors to have the benefits of the mineral waters. This vote is to build a bath house to replace that which was destroyed by fire last spring.
Is there any revenue derived from it ?
Yes, there is a fee charged to visitors, but I do not think the revenue is sufficient to maintain It.
I should think that a very excellent bath-house could be built for a smaller sum.
We have the report of the resident engineer at Calgary, and I see that it includes a cottage for the caretaker.

The right hon. gentleman was recently rather horrified at the idea of the government owning hotels and, sending agents to canvas for freight throughout the country, but he seems to have no objection to the government undertaking to operate a bath-house. Will the right hon. gentleman point out the difference between the government operating an hotel and their operating a bath-house ?
The bath is to wash away their iniquities.
If there is any difference between the government operating a bath-house and a government operating an hotel, I would like my right hon. friend to explain.

I can only explain that we do not go into this undertaking for business purposes ; it is simply an expensive luxury.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. I suppose it is on the principle that as you own the bath you must have a house over it.

Perhaps.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Is this building to be erected adjacent to the basin ?
The bath-house itself is to be a special building.
What is the salary of the caretaker ?
I cannot tell what his salary is, but he has no revenue outside of it.
Has he any duties in addition to attending to the bath ?

Yes ; the caretaker, Mr. Douglas, has a general supervision of the whole park and of the public buildings which we have there. What I would consider one of the most important of his duties is that he takes care of the animals. We have a valuable herd of buffalo, which now numbers -forty head, and which is steadily increasing I am glad to say. We have some moose and some wapita, and he looks after these.
Is this building to be erected by contract, and will it be given to the lowest tenderer ?
That is a question which might be asked the Minister of Public Works, but I should think he will answer in the affirmative, because it will cost over $5,000, and that is the law.
Will private circulars be sent around, or will it be advertised in the newspapers ?

Not in the newspapers of Banff, but elsewhere.
Amount required for the expenses in connection with the Alaskan boundary commission, $140,000.

$50,000 has
been already voted, and this will make a total appropriation of $190,000.
How is the cost arrived at ?

It will cost a large sum of money, because lawyers are expensive-my hon. friend belongs to the profession, and he knows that by experience. The class of lawyers we have had to employ must be paid high fees. Then we have had a very large staff in the preparation of the case, and my hon. friend will agree with me, if he has read the case, that it has been prepared with great care, and reflects credit on those who had charge of it. I do not yet know what will be the result of our efforts, but when the details are brought down I think it will be found that the money lias been as economically expended as it could be.

There is no doubt that able counsel were selected on the Canadian side and that a good selection was made. I do not know that I am able to say so much for one, at least, of the commissioners, if the statements attributed to him have been correctly reported. I do not wish to say anything at this stage reflecting on this gentleman. I understand that he has made some sort of a denial of the report, but not such an absolute and emphatic denial as we would have expected. If that gentleman has been correctly reported, he certainly has given expression to very unwise utterances for a man occupying such a high judicial opinion. This is not a party question, and we do not want to make it a party question ; we are all alike interested that the honour and dignity of our country should be maintained to the highest degree. It is a matter of peculiar regret to me, as a member of the same profession to which that gentleman belongs, that the report should be sent broadcast through the world that he should so far forget his duties and responsibilities as a member of that very high tribunal ; perhaps no higher tribunal has ever been created in the world of a judicial character than the tribunal of which that gentleman is a member. It is a most unfortunate incident if that gentleman is correctly reported.

For my part, I do not believe that Mr. Aylesworth has given any such interview as that which has been reported. The misfortune is that such a report should ever have got into the press, but my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) is aware that it would not be the first time that false reports have been published in the press, at-437i
tributing statements to public men, and which reports had not the slightest foundation in fact. Not later than yesterday I had to give the negation of no less a person than the Lord Chief Justice of England, who stated that a certain report made about him was a pure fabrication. The undue liberty that has been taken with the name of the Chief Justice of England may well have been taken also with the name of Mr. Aylesworth ; but I am sure that my hon. friend will readily believe that Mr. Aylesworth would be unable to so far forget himself and his duty to his profession as to be guilty of such an indiscretion as that. When a man has been at the bar the length of time that Mr. Aylesworth has, even though he has not attained Mr. Ayles-worth's eminence in his profession, he would not so comment on a matter before the judges, especially when he is one of the judges himself. For my part, therefore, I absolutely discredit the report.

The only thing that would seem to lend some possible credence to what has been suggested in the press is that the report of the proceedings of Monday seem to have been cabled to London; and, while the government have a telegram from Lord Alverstone denying the interview with him, Mr. Aylesworth has not seen fit to send any contradiction. Perhaps I should not attach too much importance to that, because it may be that the telegram to the London newspapers has not been brought to his attention. If it had been, and if the interview was uot as reported, it would have been a prudent and wise thing for Mr. Aylesworth to have followed the example of Lord Alverstone and sent a telegram to this government denying what I would call the impropriety of granting an interview of that character, with regard to a subject which is not only under the consideration of a tribunal of which he is a member, but which is also a matter of political controversy in the mother country at the present time. I would like to ask the government what the arrangements are with regard to the British counsel to represent Canada, Sir Robert Finlay and Sir Edward Carson. Are these counsel paid by the government of Canada, or are their services given ex-officio as law officers of the crown ?

Sir Robert Finlay has been selected by the British government, and, so far as my memory serves me, he is to be paid by the British government itself. I do not think this would apply to Sir Edward Carson, who was selected by us to replace Mr. Blake, who unfortunately became ill and had to give up. his position.
I do not think the cases and counter cases submitted on behalf of the two governments have been laid on the Table of the House.
I do not think they have.

There is a claim and a counter claim and a ease and a counter case, and there are appendices to these documents, and I think a set of atlases which accompany the case and the counter case. It seems to me that it would be well to have these laid on the Table of the House, and also a print of the proceedings of the committee from day to day, if my right lion, friend has it, either during the present session, or in another session, so that they will be available for reference by the members of the House. I do not know whether it is proposed to print any portion of the proceedings of this committee for distribution among the members of the House or to form a part of the sessional papers. I think that matter might well be taken into consideration by the government, as sometimes it is not convenient to get them in any other way. For example, I do not know where one can get at the proceedings of the Behring Sea tribunal except by referring to the one set of the proceedings which is in the library.

I am not aware that the proceedings of the Behring Sea commission were ever printed by this parliament. The only edition of these proceedings, so far as my memory goes, was that issued by the committee itself, a copy of which is in the library. I will take care that all the proceedings of the present tribunal be laid before the House. They will be too voluminous to print, but a good selection of them will be made for future reference, and will be referred to the committee on printing.
Has the Prime Minister had any communication from Mr. Ayles-wortli since these statements were made V
No, I have not had any.

That in itself would seem to lend some colour to this report. I am very loath to believe that a member of the bar, and so distinguished a member of the Canadian bar as Mr. Aylesworth, should make the statements which he is reported to have made. But the fact that these statements have been published, not only in the press of Canada but in the English press, must have called his attention to the fact of these statements having been circulated. Not only that, but I understand that a legal friend in Toronto, as soon as these statements appeared in the Canadian press, at once communicated them to him in England, assuming that they were not published there, so that a prompt and emphatic denial of them should be made by Mr. Aylesworth; and it has not been made. It seems to me that the First Minister should take some steps to ascertain from Mr. Ayles-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: worth himself, by communicating with him, whether or not he made these statements. This matter concerns not only Mr. Aylesworth but the whole people of Canada, whose special representative he was on that committee. Therefore it does seem to me that we should at once, if the gentleman did make those statements, take some means of bestowing upon him censure for having so far forgotten himself.

For my part, Mr. Speaker, I am not prepared to take the view of my hon. friend. My hon. friend himself, I think, would hesitate to take that view. He has been in public life for some years, and he knows that life is too short to give attention to everything that is published in the newspapers. If we were to do that, I suppose there would be nothing to do but to write items in the newspapers and give contradictions to them. I rather think that a man of Mr. Aylesworth's eminence knows his business, and knows it too well to have committed himself in that way.

It is not a case of ordinary misrepresentation-not that sort of misrepresentation which a man who is in public life is able to ignore. There is a class of misrepresentation which we do ignore. If we did not, we would be constantly defending ourselves from attacks which are unworthy of notice; but this is not a case of that character. I am loath to believe that these statements were ever made by Mr. Aylesworth but it was his duty, as representing Canada, to at once disclaim having made any such statements. Lord Alver-stone considered the matter of sufficient importance to wire the right hon. the First Minister denying that he had ever said anything which would lead Mr. Aylesworth or anybody else to the conclusion that he proposed to sacrifice Canada on behalf of the United States. If Lord Alverstone deemed it necessary to send such a denial, was it not more important that Mr. Aylesworth should also send a disclaimer ? Nothing having been heard from Mr. Aylesworth would lead one to conclude that there might be only too much truth in the report. I am loath to believe it, because Mr. Aylesworth is a distinguished Canadian, and because I am an humble member of the same profession to which he belongs. But I cannot understand his silence

I can well understand the silence of Mr. Aylesworth. If he has any duty to perform at present it is to take no notice of the wild rumours published by the reporters in London. It is his only duty to stand by his own country and try to convince his fellow commissioners that our contention is right.
That is a reflection on Lord Alverstone, who is a much more distinguished man.
He referred to the matter because it was brought up in the House of Commons in England.
The telegram which was sent referred to the discussion in the House of Commons, not only with regard to Mr. Aylesworth, but to Lord Alver-stone.

These unfortunate telegrams give rise to the necessity for his House to question whether we have pursued a wise policy in giving $15,000 a year for our Canadian press service. The Yankee service is bad, but if it is always twisted it is clear. There is some sense in its telegrams. They have a Yankee colouring but are intelligible. Since we have had this new7 service, I have read with utter disgust the nonsense that is telegraphed-utter and absolute nonsense, and I was in no particular surprised that this despatch relating to Lord Alverstone and Mr. Aylesworth should have been sent. At the same time I think that Lord Alverstone did the correct thing. It would be very extraordinary indeed that a British chief justice, acting in a very high capacity, would say the tilings attributed to Lord Alverstone. However, while members of the House of Commons would not believe it, other people, who have not the same training, possibly would.
Some members of the House of Commons seem to be the only ones who want to believe it.
Undoubtedly there are hundreds of thousands in Canada who believe it.
The hon. gentleman is mistaken. Only a few- members want to believe it, and nobody outside.

There are many people in the United States who believe it. The chief justice did the correct thing. When this statement was given world-wide publicity there was no other course for him to take than the one he did. Mr. Aylesworth should follow his example more particularly because there was considerable circumstantiality in the nonsense attributed to him. It was circumstantial in every particular. While I regard the despatch as utterly unfounded, still I was amazed at the circumstantiality which the correspondent put into it. In ordinary matters, no doubt, Mr. Aylesworf h's course would be the correct one, but this is not an ordinary matter. It involves national relations. The thing is world-wide, and it seems to me that the right hon. the First Minister would be well advised to suggest to Mr. Aylesworth to make a contradiction in equally wide terms as that of Lord Alverstone. I regard this Alaska boundary question as of great consequence to the future welfare of Canada
and the British empire. If anything untoward or anything which would give rise to a suspicion of unfairness should occur, it will shake the confidence of the Canadian people in British jurists, diplomatists and statesmen for all time. Therefore I would like these men to put themselves right in the eyes of the public, in order that there should be no feeling of any kind in Canada, previous to the making of the award, -which might lead to a charge of impropriety afterwards. Parliament voted $15,000 for a press association service, so that we are in a measure responsible for the cablegrams we get from England and ought to exercise control. and the man who sent that stuff should be summarily dismissed. He is not fit to be out of a lunatic asylum.

I should certainly not feel inclined to follow the suggestion that I should wire Mr. Aylesworth for a denial of the words attributed to him.
I want hon. gentlemen sitting here to remember that we should have some regard to what is the duty and the character of a public man. Public men to-day on whatever side of politics are simply the victims of the mad craving for sensational articles which characterizes modern journalism.
I believe that.

For my part.
I refuse steadily to deny things attributed to me without foundation. A year ago when I left New York for England, I found that the New York papers were filled with interviews attributed to me with regard to the Alaska boundary, whereas, as a matter of fact, I always denied every interviewer who called on me. As I came on deck, these men waylaid me without any shame and asked me to give them an interview. And, although I said I would not be interviewed, still interviews with me were published. I would not take the trouble to deny such things. They were not true. It is time that public men should not be held responsible except for what they utter themselves otherwise some time or other they will have to take this position. They will have to deny responsibility for anything attributed to them in the papers unless it bears such a character as makes it sure it comes from them. The chief justice, in my opinion, in the abundance of his caution, went out of his way to deny the statement attributed to him. Nobody thinks more of him because of that denial; no one would have thought the less of him if he had not made it. Nobody would have thought him capable of such an indiscretion. He thought it worth while no doubt to make a denial because there had been persistent statements in the American press to the effect that he was going to give away the case. Even the Canadian papers have been indiscreet enough to repeat such statements which have been continually in the American press the last two months. Perhaps on that ac-

count lie thought he should at once take this opportunity of nailing down such a calumny, but he had no call to do so for everybody knows the statement was false.

The right hon. the Prime Minister has said that no one believes Lord Alverstone was going to give away our case. He must have forgotten his Canadian history. He must have forgotten that practically every Canadian case was given away, and there is a very strong suspicion
What about the fishery award ?

In nearly all cases. My hon. friend knows his history as well as I do, because he began reading it a long time before I did. That is a fact, and when this appeared in the public press there was a great deal of anxiety in the minds of ordinary Canadian citizens far and wide, and it afforded pleasure to the people and showed great wisdom on his part that Lord Alverstone sent that message. Not that any one who knows Lord Alverstone, not that the Prime Minister of Canada or any citizen who really considers the position Lord Alverstone occupies, thinks that that message would make any difference in his decision, but if his decision were to be against Canada, it is fortunate that he sent that message, and if it is for Canada, it is fortunate he sent it, because it will help to allay that unfortunate feeling of unrest that exists in the minds of the public of Canada, when they think of the manner in which they have been used in the past in treaty matters.
At one o'clock, Committee took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.

When we rose at one o'clock, Mr. Chairman, we were discussing questions arising out of certain cablegrams respecting alleged utterances of Mr. Aylesworth. For my own part, I am still inclined to take the view that language of this kind could not be uttered by Mr. Aylesworth, although I appreciate the force of what has been said by some hon. gentlemen in this House that a little uncertainty is created by the fact that he has not followed the example of Lord Alverstone. I appreciate, of course, what my right hon. friend has said as to the impossibility of men in public life giving attention to every case in which they are misrepresented ; I have said twice during this session that any public man who would undertake to do that would not have much time for anything else. But a situation of this kind is a little out of the usual course. We are dealing with delicate international relations, and possibly it might be a case, in fact it is a case, where the rule to which my right hon. friend has referred might have been departed from by Mr. Aylesworth, if this telegram has been brought to his attention.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We must not, of course, overlook the fact that he possibly knows nothing about this telegram. Since we rose at one o'clock, I observe a telegram from London from which it appears that Lord Alverstone has made some reference to discussions in this House. The language of the telegram is as follows :
Lord Chief Justice Alverstone in replying after referring to the death of Sir Michael Herbert. said that though the tribunal was not an illustration of arbitration it was 'an honest and patriotic attempt to solve by mutual discussion subjects which might become serious. I have no fault to find with anything that has been said and done. We have proceeded with great unanimity and I only wish that those who do not understand the motives of the tribunal would abstain from attributing motives to its members which do not exist.'
This open reference to Canadian criticism of Lord Alverstone's supposed pre-disposition towards the American case caused no little sensation. It was followed by Lord Alvestone somewhat passionately declaring that in a long public career he had never objected to criticism after he had taken a certain course of action but he did bitterly resent criticism beforehand.
So far as this parliament is concerned- and the reference by Lord Alverstone seems to me to matters that have been mentioned in this parliament-I think that all the members of this House should agree with me that not the slightest attempt to criticise Lord Alverstone has been made here. The only reference to him was made by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) who brought to the attention of the government a certain telegram which was sent out from a reputable source in London, and on being assured by the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce that in his opinion no attention should be paid to a rumour of that kind, my hon. friend (Mr. Bell) made no further reference to the subject and accepted as absolutely satisfactory the view of the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. I think it is perhaps right for us to say this lest there should be any impression in the mind of Lord Alverstone or any one else that there has been in this parliament the slightest suggestion of criticism upon any action which his Lordship has taken since he was appointed one of the commissioners to sit on this tribunal on behalf of Great Britain.

I certainly endorse every word of my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax). Nothing has been said which reflected in any way upon Lord Alverstone. For my own part, I still persist in believing that even the report which has just been read by my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) of the remarks of Lord Alverstone have been highly coloured.
Very likely.

I repeat that I cannot believe Lord Alverstone could take offence at anything that has been said here.

Additional amount required to assist in defraying coat of the publication of documents issued by the Canadian Mining Institute, $2,000.

Might I ask whether or not the proceedings of the institute are distributed ? Are they sent to members of parliament or to any public bodies ? It is a very desirable object, I believe, to assist this work, although the increase is a very substantial one. Possibly it would not be impossible to make some condition as to the distribution.

Speaking under correction, but I am sure that I am right,
I may say that these reports to which we are now contributing this sum are sent to all public libraries, and I think they are also sent abroad.
Amount required to cover expenses connected with land slide at Turtle Mountain, $8,000.

This grant is made necessary in order to undo the great damage which was caused by the flood at Frank. The House will remember that during the present session, I think it was in the month of May, in consequence of a very serious flood after great rains which took place at Dead Man's river, a part of Turtle mountain was thrown into the river, which accident threatened the collieries at Frank, and we had to send a force to that place in order to remove the debris and make a passage for the water. This is to cover that expenditure.
Additional amount required for expenses of the Assay office in British Columbia, $1,000.
I think I understood from the right hon. gentleman the other day that the real effect of this was to give an increase of $100.

I was mistaken. It is an increase of $400.
Dominion Lands-charge-able to income-further amount required for salaries of the outside service, $10,000.

This is to provide for an increase in the outside service, and chiefly for clerical work in the different land offices in the North-west Territories. The clerical staff has to be increased on account of the great increase of work which has taken place in the various land offices. I was asked to give some information upon this subject the other day. During the first nine months of 1902 the number of free homestead entries was 15,983. For the same nine months of the present year the number of free homestead entries has risen to 36,882. The arrivals during the first nine months of 1902 were 68,802, and the arrivals during the first nine months of the present year were 108,014.

Bast year I drew attention to the fact that a great many of the settlers coming in and taking up homesteads were unmarried men. You cannot force a man to marry, but you can encourage him to marry. I want to say that it is my opinion, based on careful observation, that a married man two years in that country is worth a single man half a dozen years
So he is everywhere.

Much more so there than anywhere else, because in other localities the young fellows have an opportunity of brushing up, they are under the influence of women in the older settled districts more than they are in the remote regions of the North-west. I think the Prime Minister could do a good service to the country by giving a man his homestead after two years provided he is a married man, and making it five years if he is a single man.
Why does not my hon. friend go further, and say that spinsters may take up homesteads, the same as in the United States ?
I think that should be a law, too.
I would go back to the practice in my own province and provide a free homestead for every man who has children.
I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman if there has been any provision made for the increase in the salary of Mr. Bennett at Strathcona ?

There has 'been no increase.
Excise-salaries of officers and inspectors of excise. &c.-further amount required to provide increase in accordance with the proposed amendment. schedule B, Inland Revenue, Civil Service Act, $12,000.
Will the Minister of Inland Revenue (Hon. Mr. Bernier) give us an explanation V

Mr. Chairman, the main estimates were made up at the beginning of the year, and this sum is to meet the increases provided for by the Bill amending the Civil Service Act which was passed to-day. I propose, with the consent of the Committee, as four mbnths of the current year have elapsed, to reduce the amount to $8,000.
