Mr, FOWLER. May I ask the hon. minister whether provision is made for raising the salary of his secretary ?
No.
How many private secretaries has the hon. minister at the present time ?
I have one secretary-Mr. Bourgault. He will receive the same increase as the other officers of the inside service under the Bill.

Do I understand that the minister has only one>
private secretary, although the civil service list credits him with three ?
There is only one private secretary ; Mr. Bourgault, of St. Hyacinthe, at $600.
Would the minister give me the names of those who received increases at Prescott, and their present salaries ?

Subject to a deduction of one-third in the figures I give, the following are the increases : Mr. Keilty, collector, salary $1,600, increase $200. Mr. Gerald is a special officer and he will receive no increase. Mr. Melville, increase $100 ; Mr. Macdonald, increase $60 ; Sir. Keeler, increase $42.50. Mr. Johnston is asking for a superannuation, but lie would be entitled to an increase of $30. and Mr. Marshall gets an increase of $30 also.
Would the minister give the increases in the office at Perth ?
Mr. McLenaghan, increase $70 ; Mr. Mason, increase $70 ; Mr. Goodman, increase $50.
Are these increases given according to length of service, or on what are they based ?

The increases of salary are based on the following plan : officers who have not yet reached the new minimum receive an increase that will bring their salaries up to that minimum as fixed by the new amend-mont to the Civil Service Act ; officers wlirr have passed the new minimum and are receiving a regular increment of 5 per cent will receive an additional amount beyond that provided in the main estimates, which makes the annual increase 5 per cent on the new minimum.
What is the present salary of Mr. Melville and Mr. Gerald ?
Mr. Melville's present salary is $1,200, and Mr. Gerald's $1,600.

In so far as the increases of salary at Prescott are concerned, a more unfair proposition could not be submitted to this House. Personally, I am glad to see these officers getting an increase of salary, but here is Mr. Gerald, who has been in the department for twenty years and who is one of the best officers in the Dominion of Canada without doubt, and who has passed his civil service examination and he gets no increase, while Mr. Keilty, who is not capable of taking the position which Mr. Gerald occupies, gets an increase of $200. Mr. Melville, whom the minister only appointed a few days ago at a salary of $1,200, gets an increase of $100 per annum, and Mr. Gerald, who has been so long in the service, gets no increase. The best man in the service to-day is Mr. Gerald. He is the most competent man in the office. Working right alongside him is Mr. Macdonald, who gets an increase of $60, and Mr. Gerald gets none. The minister tries to get out of this by saying that Mr. Gerald is a special officer, but he has passed all examinations and he is the chief excise man there, and there is no question that he is one of the best men in the Dominion of Canad to-day. It may have been that Mr. Gerald's brother, who is the deputy minister, has hesitated in recommending an increase, but it is a most unfair thing that the other officers should get increases and that Mr. Gerald, who has been twenty years in the department, should get no increase. I do not object to these other gentlemen getting increases, and I am glad to see that they do, but there should be fair-play all
round. While on this point, I wish to express regret that the Minister of Customs has not taken a vote to increase the salaries of his officers at Prescott, because they are all hard-working officials and they should have got increases. I appeal to the Minister of Inland Revenue, to add to this vote an increase of $200 for Mr. Gerald, and I may say that there is not a Liberal in the town of Prescott who would not recommend that being done.

I am free to admit that Mr. Gerald is one of the best officers we have in the province of Ontario. He had an increase of $100 in his salary from the 1st of -Tnlv and lip hns-received every year $150 of what we call duty pay in addition to his salary. Though Mr. Gerald is a very capable man, the law does not allow us to give him more. The list was prepared by the deputy of the department. He knows the law, and I am informed by him that we could not do better than we have done. With regard to the deputy collector, he is, of course, a new man ; but he has received the salary to which be is entitled under the law. There is a minimum, and maximum fixed, and it is the custom of the department to give a fair remuneration to the officers. These increases have been given in order to raise the minimum of each class as it is prescribed by the amended Act.

The hon. minister is now leading us to believe that in giving the deputy collector this increase, he is doing what is fair all round. Why did he not deal with the officers entitled to an increase in the town of Prescott ? He had a deputy collector in the town of Prescott before he appointed the present one five or six days ago. Why was his salary not brought up to the salary of the present deputy collector ? This man is ahead of the other, so far as promotion is concerned; but the other was appointed to evade the Civil Service Act, and he has since passed the examination. One of these deputy collectors in the town of Prescott has received an increase of $100, though appointed less than a month ago, and has $1,300 per annum. Will the hon. minister explain why he dis-' criminates between the two ?

The hon. gentleman refers to Mr. White. He was appointed deputy collector class B. He has not passed his examination, and therefore it is not in our power to raise his salary. If I were to increase the salaries of all the deputy collectors in class B in one locality, I woud have to do the same all over the Dominion. I have tried to equalize the salaries as well as I could. It is no fault of the department if Mr. White had not taken the precaution to qualify j himself. I have nothing to say^ against 1 him ; he is a good officer ; but he is not in

a position, to perform the duties of deputy collector in class A, or those of Mr. Gerald.

When Mr. White was appointed two or three years ago, he was appointed deputy collector to evade the Civil Service Act, and at the present time he is filling the position of exciseman. In this way the law is evaded. Was the collector in class A when he was promoted ?
Yes, he was collector in class A, and he had passed the promotion examination.
In the list of increases which the bon. minister has read, is there any deputy collector in class B who has any increase?
No, none.

I asked the minister a question respecting private secretaries. He stated that there was only one, Mr. Alphonse Bourgault. I see that the civil service list gives his name and two others, Napoleon Potvin and Robert Peter Yetts. Besides, I understand that the minister has an assistant secretary, Miss Chevrier, one of the famous Chevrier family who are so numerous in the civil service. Will the bon. minister say why he has these three private secretaries ?	.

I am not responsible for misprints. Mr. Alphonse Bourgault is my private secretary, but the others are messengers. Napoleon Potvin has never been my private secretary, and Mr. Yetts is a messenger. He has never been a private secretary.
It is strange that there should be any misprints. In the first place, I do not sete why this office should require three messengers.
There were three in the department, and one was transferred to the laboratory branch.
The hon. gentleman states that Mr. Johnston has applied for superannuation. Has that been . granted yet ?
No, but I have prepared a recommendation for it at his own request.
Has any other gentleman been recommended for the position ?
No.
I understood that another officer had applied for superannuation.
No. Mr. Ferguson was superannuated at his own request about three months ago.
Has Mr. Bisset passed the examination ?
No, he is a temporary officer.
Is he likely to hold that position permanently if he does not pass the examination ?
No. He has been told, like everybody else in the department who has not complied with the law, to present himself for examination in the month of November next.
Suppose he fails in the examination ?
Then I suppose we shall have to keep him there for a certain time, and he will run his risk.

The hon. minister is evading the Civil Service Act; and when i brought the fact to his attention, he tried to make out that there was nothing in it. He has appointed a man to that position who never passed the civil service examination and never will. The hon. minister admits that if he fails next November to pass, he will still be kept on. And if he should fail the following November, he will still be continued in office indefinitely. I have heard it discussed throughout the constituency that the hon. gentleman has agreed to appoint preventive officers and promote preventive officers to collectors without any examination whatever. That is unfair to those who have passed their examinations.

The hon. gentleman has gone a little too far. I have said already that there were two doors open by which appointments could be made without the applicants passing an examination. One is to appoint deputy collectors and the other temporary officers. These temporary officers are not appointed by Order in Council but by letter sent to the collector, telling him to employ a man temporarily at a stated salary. If my hon. friend is so anxious to have the law respected, he should go back some twenty years and he will find that almost every department had then and has still men who never passed their examination. This Mr. Bissell was appointed just the same as other temporary officers. He was not appointed to fill the position left vacant by Mr. Ferguson, but if he qualifies himself he will be entitled to take that position. If he does not do his duties properly or if he cannot pass the examination, he will have to resign; but if that rule be applied a great many officials, who are friends of the party opposite and who were appointed by them, would have to be dismissed.

The hon. gentleman asked me to go back twenty years,

but we are dealing with the present, and I am not referring to any constituency but the one I represent. I challenge him to name one instance in the county of Grenville, while the Conservatives were in power, in which the law was evaded. What I am asking is not unfair. If he appoints any person to a vacant position and that person cannot pass the civil service exami-tion, he ought to withdraw and give the place to someone who can pass it. The hon. minister proposes to let that man go on indefinitely, whether he passes or not. The hon. minister will have an Order in Council passed appointing the man as preventive officer. Will he say that if this man to whom I refer should fail in his ex animation, he will not continue in office 1

If I were to apply the law the hon. gentleman would find it would hurt his own supporters more than anybody else. There are many gentlemen who support the party opposite who have been years in office but for one reason or another have never passed the examination; and if the hon. gentleman wants the rule to be applied to all departments he takes the responsibility of urging that perhaps 200 or more temporary officers, who have been in the service many years, will be dismissed. I am not not ready to say that there is one in the constituency represented by the hon. gentleman who has not complied with the law ; but should there be one, it would not be prudent, or in the interests of that gentleman, that we should bring his name forward, because he is exactly in the same position as many others who are not disturbed.

The hon. minister led us to believe that he was going to have a better staff and make improvements and have everything in better shape. Is it a sample of his improvements that he will appoint men to positions who cannot pass the examination ? Because that was done in the past is no excuse for doing it now. 1 understood from the hon. minister that he was going to stand by the Civil Service Act, and I think it is a very poor excuse to say that because his predecessors made appointments of this kind, he is going to continue the same thing. I am not asking for the dismissal of any officer who has been in the service for years, but I do not want him to appoint men on the staff whether they can pass the examination or not. There are plenty of men in my constituency who have passed the examination and who are just as good Liberals as the man you have appointed. If the hon. minister is going to continue a policy of this kind, there will be no object for young men to pass the civil service examination, because all they will need to get positions will be a recommendation from the Liberal committee, even if they cannot read or write.
Is the hon. gentleman able to give me the name of a man in Prescott who cannot sign his name ?

I did not say that there was an officer in Prescott who could not write his name. I say that if any man in the county of Grenville can secure the recommendation of the Liberal committee to a vacancy in the Inland Revenue Department, whether he can write his name or not, the hon. minister will appoint him and evade the law.
To increase the salaries of the inspectors of distilleries, inspector of bonded factories, inspector of tobacco factories, and-inspector of malt houses and breweries, not exceeding $300 in any one case, $1,200.

As the Committee will see, no increase in salary was provided for the inspectors in the different divisions of the Dominion. We have -eight of those divisions in the Dominion-one in British Columbia, one in Manitoba, three in Ontario, two in Quebec and one in the lower provinces. Before the position of assistant commissioner was abolished three years ago, the gentleman who held that position, the present deputy minister, acted at the same time as inspector of tobacco, manufactories, distilleries, breweries, &c. Since the positions of commissioner and assistant commissioner were abolished the duties of the deputy minister were such that he could not attend to the duties required from the inspector. Mr. Barrett, of Winnipeg, is inspector of breweries and malt houses ; Mr. Kenning, of Windsor, is inspector of dis-stilleries ; Mr. -Stratton is inspector of bonded factories. The inspector of tobacco factories has not yet been appointed, but he will be chosen from the best qualified district inspectors in the province of Quebec, and probably Mr. Lawlor will be appointed as such inspector. The jurisdiction of these inspectors will be over all Canada, and the increase will take effect from January or sooner. The present maximum salary of the inspectors is $2,500.

It seems to me that these gentlemen are well provided for now with $2,500 and expenses. Why are the words added :
Not to exceed $300 in any one case ?

We are not bound to give all of that increase in the same year, that will be the maximum of their salaries. We have amon-g these gentlemen some who have not yet reached the present maximum of their salaries. '

By this provision you are taking into the hands of the minister power to do just the thing to which objection has -been taken, -give increases on

grounds of favouritism to men who have not fulfilled the conditions which, under the Act, entitles them to an increase. These increases should be statutory and should not be at the discretion of the minister, subject, I presume, to the recommendation of the deputy minister. I make no reflection upon the minister or his deputy. I assume that these gentlemen are the same as ordinary mortals, with the same infirmities, moved by the same impulses, and I say that you are putting that power Into the hands of the minister of the deputy to discriminate between officers who may ibe equally worthy. It gives an opportunity for a great deal of unfairness, and should not be sanctioned.
These officers, Mr. Kenning, Mr. Barrett, Mr. Stratton and Mr. Lawlor, are officers of long standing and capacity in the department.
I am not saying anything against the officers. I do not know anything about these gentlemen, I assume that they are worthy men.

I give this information, because some persons might suppose that undue favour was being shown to these officers. Mr. Lawlor has been in the service as collector at Montreal for fifteen or seventeen years. Last year he was promoted to the office of inspector, with a salary of $2,300. whereas he was only getting $2,200 as collector. The position of inspector may be transferred from one man to another man. The first gentleman appointed inspector was Mr. Gow. Some two years ago he retired and was superannuated, and was succeeded by Mr. Kenning who was collector at Windsor, and one of the oldest officers in the department. Mr. Stratton held a similar position for many years, as did also Mr. Barrett. Wlfen another man is appointed he will be entitled like these gentlemen to receive an additional $300. If any of these gentlemen were to retire or were to be replaced by some others, their salary would be reduced, because the salary is attached to the position and not to the person himself. This $300 is given to the gentlemen, whoever they are, who fulfil the duties of inspector of breweries, distilleries, tobacco manufactories and so forth.

If that be the case why does the hon. gentleman want power to make a distinction ? If the salary belongs to the office and not to the incumbent, why does he want to make a distinction ? Toil say these four men are to be selected from the eight officers who are now fulfilling certain duties. What additional service do these four men have to give in order to entitle them to receive an increase over the other four men who are left behind ? Is it because they are travelling inspectors that they require more salary ? That is a reason against it. because if you pay, this Mr. FOWLER.
man's expenses, if he is travelling all the time you pay all his living expenses. He is not at the expense of living at home. If he were at home he would have to pay his own board. The person who remains at home really requires more salary than the officer who is constantly travelling. I can not see any justification in anything the minister has said in favour of this increase.

This practice has prevailed ever since I have been at the head of the department. These special inspectors will be chosen among the best officers, and we consider the best officers are those whose capacity and long training have fitted them for the first positions in the service, that is to say, district inspectors. Of course, there will be four men who will not benefit by this special allowance, but there has been no discrimination shown. I had to appoint two, Mr. Kennie and Mr. Lawlor, and they were chosen among the oldest officers on the staff.	The
other four will wait until these gentlemen disappear by death or otherwise. It may be said that it is not fair to choose between them. But we hold out an inducement for those who aspire to be district inspectors to qualify themselves to fulfil the duties of an inspector for a special industry. The hon. member must remember that these gentlemen must possess not only qualifications of a special character which enable them to fulfil the duties of inspector in their own division, but they must go all through the Dominion and inspect all these various manufactories, and inspect the books. There fore they must possess a technical knowledge. I do not see that there is any injustice in saying to these inspectors who are younger : Wait for a while until these gentlemen who are now your superiors disappear, and then, if the same salary is still provided by parliament, you will have your opportunity of rising and getting the $300 additional. This $300 is only a small reward for those who receive no increase of salary. I find by looking at the schedule of salaries that the salaries of the inspectors have not been increased, they remain at $2,500, while the other officers, the collectors and deputy collectors, accountants and so forth, are receiving increases.

The minister says it is uot the intention to give the salary to the man but to the position. Supposing the inspector of a distillery was removed and went back to his old position, then he would lose the additional salary which is attached to the former position.
He would lose a portion of the $300.

If it be the case that the salary goes to the office and not to the individual. why should there be that discrimination between the positions ? Is not the position of inspector of distilleries as impor-

tant as that of inspector of bonded factories, of tobacco factories, or malt houses and breweries ? Why, make any distinction between the positions in respect to salaries ?

There is no discrimination with regard to salaries. I have stated that we can do one thing or another. The intention is to give these gentlemen $300, and we ask for that amount, but we are not bound to give it. I have explained that there is no discrimination, that in the case of Mr. Lawlor, for instance, he is inspector of the largest and most important districts in the whole Dominion. He is the inspector, lint, as he in fl-new officer, he is only receiving $2,300. I said that we proposed to give him $300, which would make his salary $2,600, and the other gentlemen would be entitled to the same amount of increase ; that is to say, $300.

That is not what I propose. I say that we are not bound to give $300 to all of them. We. might begin at $100, or $200, or we might make it $300, but if one receives $100 the others will receive $100, and there will be no discrimination.
And no more ?
And no more.
That is satisfactory. The hon. minister did not say that before.

We cannot change the scale of salaries now paid to those officers who are occupying positions as inspectors. We do not propose to change the salaries of those who receive $2,500. I have taken the case of Mr. Lawlor, because he is only receiving $2,300, as he was recently appointed, and if we give $100, $200 or $300 to one, the other three will receive the same increase.

As the hon. minister has made that statement, as far as the division of the money is concerned, it is perfectly satisfactory. At the same time, I protest against the increase at all, because I do not
think there should be an increase. I do not think the fact that they are travelling men should entitle them to an increase.

As far as Prescott is concerned, I would make one more appeal to the hon. minister. Mr. ICeilty receives $1,300 and Mr. Gerald $1,500. The hon. minister states that Mr. Gerald is to receive $1,600 and that Mr. Keilty will receive $1,600. Mr. Gerald is a special officer, he has a large family to support, it is very expensive living there, and as I think he should have an increase I would be very glad if the hon. minister could see his way clear to give nim one. We could pass it now. He is a special officer, and there is no reason why he should not get an increase with the rest. He is really the head of the staff at Prescott. He is the main officer there and he is entitled to a little increase. If the hon. minister would consent to give him an iuerease I do not think it would be unfair, and I think every officer in Prescott would be glacf to see him get an increase with the rest. I hope the hon. minister will see his way clear to grant him an increase.

I regret that I cannot change the law, although I am ready to appreciate that Mr. Gerald is one of the best officers in the service. Mr. Gerald is entitled to a $100 increase from the 1st of July. He received it. Next year he will be entitled to $100 more and he will receive it. I cannot change the schedule of the Act.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And he has $150 from another source.
Yes. I think he is entirely satisfied. My authority for speaking in that way, is that the gentleman who applies the law is a brother of Mr. Gerald, of Prescott.

I am very sorry, but I understood that the law was such that in the case of a special officer the department could give him any salary they wished. I think, if the hon. minister could see his way clear to evade the law in other instances, he could have seen his way clear to have got around it in this case.
What salary has Mr. Nash, the inspector of Inland Revenue in Prince Edward Island ?
One thousand two hundred dollars, and be will receive $60 of an increase according to the amended schedule that forms part of the Civil Service Act.

I desire to bring to the notice of the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue the fact that I spoke to him a few days ago in regard to the claim of Mr. O'Rielly, whose factory was burned and whose tobacco had to be supplied from the

139S0
outside. Will the hon. minister state if Mr. O'Rielly is to be compensated ?
I am told by my deputy that this claim was discussed, and that there is no legal ground for entertaining the same.

There may be no legal grounds for it, but there are moral grounds. Mr. O'Rielly's tobacco factory was destroyed by fire after the place was stocked for the winter season. The hon. minister will find that the revenue derived from this factory this year was more than the previous year, and I trust that he will see that Mr. O'Rielly is compensated for the loss he sustained in the fire.

I would not like to pass judgment on the case of Mr. O'Rielly. The facts are these : There was a certain quantity of tobacco destroyed by fire. I presume that this gentleman had some insurance on the premises and on the goods, but the law says that no refund can be made on goods destroyed by fire after the duty is paid. The goods were in store in Mr. O'Rielly's factory. They were destroyed, and we are not able, because thei law prevents us, to give any refund to the gentleman. I presume this has been discussed somewhere, and although the department would be willing to help Mr. O'Rielly to the best of its ability, we cannot do it under the law as it is now.
Have you not already allowed Mr. O'Rielly a certain amount of compensation for this loss ?

Yes, but the cases are quite different. In one instance he was allowed to pass a free entry to cover goods destroyed in bond but when the goods have been entered and the duty paid we are not allowed to refund the money.
Were these goods destroyed in the bonded warehouse or in the factory?
In his tobacco factory.
There is a bonded warehouse which is a part of each factory. Were these goods in that bonded warehouse or outside of the bonded warehouse in the factory ?

If the goods are destroyed before duty is paid he has not to pay the duty ; but. when the goods were destroyed in his factory or warehouse as was the case in Prince Edward Island, they were his property and should have been insured.
They were not in the bonded warehouse ?

No.
Salaries and contingent expenses of the several ports in Canada-additional amount required for salaries (including pay for overtime of officers, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act), $100,000.

When the main estimates were under consideration I explained that the government would in future pay officers who are engaged for extra service at railway stations and such. This has been a charge on the transportation companies hitherto, and for many years past they have been representing that it should be a charge on the revenue of the Dominion.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The minister fully explained this before.

This vote is well worded when it speaks of working ' overtime ' and the ' outside service.' Would it include the salary of H. L. Pelletier, who is employed hi the customs house in Montreal, and who works overtime canvassing for ' Le Canada ' ?
There is a gentleman named H. E. Pelletier in the Montreal office.

That is the gentleman. Does the minister know he is canvassing for ' Le Canada ' in the country districts and that he has been spending some three weeks in the county of Chateauguay in that mission ? Would that come under the heading of 'overtime' or 'outside service'?

No. This is the first I have heard of that matter, but I can assure the hon. gentleman that Mr. Pelletier will not be paid out of this vote. I do not know whether Mr. Pelletier may have been doing some work during his holidays.

I understand that Mr. Latour, an officer of the Public Works Department, got six months leave of absence on account of ill health, his son taking his place, and that he is also an agent for ' Le Canada ' through the province of Quebec. I have often heard the Minister of Customs in his eloquent and able and sometimes loud manner. denounce public officers for doing political work, and if Mr. Pelletier, who is drawing a salary from the government is canvassing for a political organ like ' Le Canada ' will the Minister of Customs take his political head off and dismiss him?
I do not know anything about the circumstances of the case, but they will be inquired into. He is a permanent officer and gets three weeks leave of absence.
When did he have his three weeks leave ?
The collector arranges that, and we have no means
of knowing. X do not think that the collector at Montreal would give Mr. Pelletier extra leave to go on a mission of that kind.
Do I understand that a permanent officer can devote himself to political work when he is on his holidays ?
Is canvassing for a newspaper ' political work ' ?
Canvassing for a government party organ.
The interference of officials in politics is not favoured, buL does canvassing ror a regular established journal come under the head of political work ?

What is the opinion of the minister on that ? During the last seven years we have had a great many dismissals "because some officers interfered but slightly in political matters, and there is no doubt that when a man is canvassing for a party organ he is probably making as much political capital as he can out of it. I know of no better introduction to a house for political work that the canvassing for a newspaper. I would like to know If the minister thinks this man has a right to do that work in his holidays ?

I would not like to express an opinion on what a man might or might not do in his holidays. As to a man being connected with a newspaper, I think complaints have been made of that in my department, and it has been recognized that we must not draw the line too strictly in that respect. As the hon. gentleman says1 he has done the work in his holidays, I would not like to say offhand that he had done wrong. I would like to inquire into the matter first.

Certainly, I would not ask the hon. minister to condemn him without inquiry. That he was canvassing there is no doubt. During his holidays he would be drawing his salary, as he is a permanent officer. Under these circumstances, how-can the minister have any doubt as to his doing partisan work ?
The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS, I am not putting it on the ground of partisan work. I am putting it on the ground that the hon. gentleman says he has been canvassing for subscriptions to a public journal. It seems to me that there is a distinction between a case of that kind and the case of an officer going out and canvassing to have votes cast for a political party. I think the hon. gentleman must see the distinction.

I would see a distinction if it were an ordinary magazine or paper that was not absolutely wrapped up in politics. But I think the minister must agree with me that a paper published as a mouthpiece
of a political party is different. If a man takes- that paper into his household, I think it is a pretty strong temptation for him to begin to canvass and talk politics for that paper. I think it is the strongest evidence that that gentleman has been working for a certain party through a certain journal ; and if it be found to be true that Mr. Pelletier was going through the country canvassing for ' De Canada,' which is recognized in the province of Quebec as a political paper published in the interest of the Liberal party, the minister should tell us whether he considers that work political work or not, and whether he intpnfis to investigate the case ?

All our papers, I suppose, might be called political papers, as they are supposed to represent the views of one party or the other. I do not want to say anything about the matter, as this is the first time that it has been brought to my notice; but the hon. gentleman having brought the matter up, I will ask the collector for a report upon it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Had not the hon. gentleman better allow this item to stand until he communicates with his officer in Montreal, and ascertain the facts ? My hon. friend says this man spent three weeks in Chateauguay county. If he has spent three weeks in every county in Quebec, he has used up all his holidays and more. The information is that he is travelling around the country doing this kind of work. The hon. minister had better ascertain when he took his leave of absence, to see whether it corresponds with the time that my hon. friend says he spent in the county of Chateauguay. Then, he brings up the case of Mr. Latour, an employee of the Public Works Department, who has been granted leave of absence and whose son has been put in his place, in order that he might become the head travelling agent for * Le Canada.' It is said that he goes to every postmaster in the country and demands from him the names of all the subscribers to Conservative newspapers which go to that office and if the postmaster refuses to give the names, he threatens him with dismissal. The government gives this man six months' leave of absence to go out and do this work: and the hon. minister now wants this vote to give this man an extra allowance for doing this political work.

I think my hon. friend is not serious in that. This vote has nothing to do with Mr. Pelletier. He is a regular officer on the Montreal staff, and is being paid out of appropriations already granted by parliament. As I have explained, the larger part of this vote is for the pay of extra officers who have previously been paid by the transportation companies.
Ts not Mr. Pelletier under the pay of the department?
Yes.
So this has nothing to do with the circumstance, because this vote does not appertain to his payment.

His pay does not come out of this ; therefore, I think there would be no necessity of letting the item stand. I will make inquiries, and if he will bring the question up on concurrence, I will tell him then what I have learned about it. The estimates of the Department of Customs are generally prepared with that regard for economy which should meet the approval of the House, and they generally go through without any very disparag ing comment.

It is all very well to talk about the estimates being prepared with due regard to economy, but the hon. members on the back benches must laugh in their sleeves when they hear the ministers discourse in this strain. We were told by these gentlemen that they would not allow the civil servants to indulge in any active partisanship and they made that the excuse for dismissing a number of them without trial, yet here we have a case of an official going through the country doing party work, and when it is brought to the attention of the hon. minister he treats it very lightly. I should like very much to find one instance in which these hon. gentlemen opposite have kept their word. Here is a case of offensive partisanship, and I ask the hon. minister to treat it as the government did the cases of many Conservatives. They dismissed any number of officials, without even giving them an opportunity of defending themselves. Yet here is a flagrant case of political partisanship and they refuse to act. Here is an official who went around the country doing the political work of his party, and he is to be paid, not out of the pockets of hon. gentlemen opposite, but out of the revenues of the country. The farmers are bled white paying officials for running around doing work which the ministers ought to do themselves. We have the Minister of Customs now, a full fledged minister, although the party he supported said that the position he holds should not have been created, and that there were too many ministers. But no sooner did they secure office than they appointed more ministers.
The hon. gentleman who 'brought up the case is satisfied with the assurance that I have given that it was the first I heard of it and that I would inquire into it.

I regret that I am not satisfied with the plea of the hon. minister.
I would have thought that, from his long training in opposition, he would have had a very live mental apprehension of what political partisanship meant and would not have found it necessary to take time to

ascertain whether a man who goes around canvassing for a political paper is a partisan or not. The hon. gentleman appears to be losing his mental intuition in these matters. I would regard it as a flagrant case of partisanship that an official should introduce among my electors a Liberal organ. What I find extraordinary is that the hon. minister could have any doubt about it. I would not mind an officer taking the stump for weeks during a violent political campaign because men's feelings are then aroused and you cannot then make a man change his political creed, but when you introduce, in times of peace, a political organ among the people, if it is intelligently written, you are introducing a very dangerous element against the party it is opposing, and I would regard the agent of that organ as a violent and a very astute political partisan. What I find extraordinary is that the minister should have any doubt.
Is there in that $100,000 any increases in Prescott ?

Yes. The whole vote will be taken up with the payment of overtime and a little extra amount for the salaries of some officers we think are deserving.
Mi-. REID (Grenville). I understand that many officers have been getting quite a little sum from the Canadian Pacific Railway for overtime at night. I think they average something between $30 and $40 which they divide amongst themselves. Has that been taken away now ? Does the government receive the revenue and then pay these officers ?

It will be paid by us and not the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Canadian Pacific Railway used to pay that sum to the collectors at the various ports who paid it to the officers for extra work. The House is now assuming the payment of these officers for overtime. We require the transportation companies still to pay something where we consider the work entirely for their own benefit. For instance we require the services of a customs officer outside of Canada at the request of the railway companies they are accommodating. They ask that for their own convenience. The Canadian Pacific Railway may ask for a Canadian customs officer at Boston, Portland or Chicago, because it is a convenience to parties passing over that road, and they can secure passengers by having that facility. We have officers in attendance on frontier highway bridges and ferries during certain seasons of the year, to be regulated by the collector, subject to the approval of the department, and then such other customs services of a special character or class as may be required on the approval of the minister himself and on the applications of the par-

ties accommodated. When a company gets the services of an officer for its own special benefit and not for the benefit of Canada, we still require them to pay. In all other cases, if parliament consents to this vote, all extra services rendered by officers, which have hitherto been defrayed toy the transportation companies, will be defrayed out of this vote.

I hope that the two officers who have been dividing the time and receiving about $40 a month will continue to receive that, either from the railway company or from the department. They are in receipt of small salaries, and that is quite an item to them.

Yes, that is the intention. In cases where officers' salaries have been supplemented by this extra service we will continue that, and they will be paid that amount, provided the hours of their day's duty before that has not been too long. We require the officers to give us the full day's time, and all services rendered after that will be paid for at 25 cents an hour. It may be that In some of the large ports which the commissioner has visited we may have to use some of this money to add an extra man or two, as it may be advisable to have night men, and we are asking for a little latitude in order that we may get this system into proper order.
Is a collector of customs at a port supposed to be in his office a certain number of hours per day ?
Yes, certainly ; offices are generally open from nine till four ; but we require all our officers to be on duty from eight to six, if business calls for it.

The Minister of Customs tells us, in a somewhat soothing tone, that every one seems to be perfectly satisfied about the charge made with respect to Mr. Pelletier, tout I hardly think we ought to be satisfied with the very vague remarks of my hon. friend with regard to that case. It seems to me a most extraordinary thing that an employee of the Department of Customs should, while drawing a salary from government, be engaged in canvassing for any newspaper, and I would think that my hon. friend himself would suggest that an item in his estimates referring to Mr. Pelletier should stand until an investigation had been held and definite and accurate information on the subject obtained and given to parliament and the people. My hon. friend seems to suggest that Mr. Pelletier had been canvassing while he was on a holiday. Would my hon. friend inform me whether or not this gentleman has any definite period for holidays ; and if so, at what season of the year ?
43S

No, there is no definite three weeks in the year to which officers of the different ports are entitled. The collector arranges so that they may go away one by one, or two at a time, as he can spare them.

The hon. minister said that I was quite satisfied with what he said ;
I am satisfied that he should investigate the question, and so far his reply was encouraging to me ; but I received no other information, and the balance of his reply gave me no satisfaction whatever. I still think that the minister should not permit such a violation of the proper conduct of an employee of his department. We know that many dismissals have taken place in the public service for alleged political actions by employees, and sometimes we can scarcely find a reason for dismissals that have taken place. Many of these men, some old and some young, have had to seek new ways for getting a living, and are suffering in consequence of either the high ideal of the hon. gentleman and his colleagues, or of the meanest sort of political ambition. I think we are entitled to know on which of these principles such dismissals have taken place. Personally, while I do not believe in officers taking any part in politics, there have been instances in my own knowledge in which the government have gone a very long way in seeking a reason for the dismissal of employees. I think the hon. minister should hold an investigation in this case, and that we should know whether the government is going to permit the employees of the departments to use their energies, while they are receiving government pay, to canvass for political newspapers ; for we know that a man who thus sows the seeds of a particular political faith in families is doing the most telling work in promoting the interests of a party. The hon. gentleman would not like to be held to the statement that there is no election in sight. He is not himself yet positive whether or not there is an election in sight. He does not know whether the government can or can not afford to have an election in the near future. The ministers have vacillated in their opinions as to the holding of an election ever since we came here on March 12th. The man who goes about as a canvasser for a political paper is doing the real work of a political organizer.
I do not know what my hon. friend thinks of the work of a man who goes out on that business. Of course, it is not the work of a man who goes forth to buy votes. But I know of no better way of spending money, if you wish to prepare a constituency, than to see that the proper newspapers which preach your political doctrines are circulated among the people in the constituency. I am not alone in having discovered that. I think the Minister of Customs is possessed of that fact as well as I am. It is well



known that every party makes a desperate effort to see that its own political organs take the place of others. Here we have a man going about for that purpose who is paid by the government-for I understand that Mr. Pelletier was in the permanent service-going about and asking the postmasters and others to give him a list of the people who get mail at their offices, and of those who take the opposition newspapers, in order to discourage the taking of the opposition papers and to encourage the taking of government organs. In my judgment this gentleman is doing most efficient political work. If he has been doing it he should be dismissed. I am satisfied the minister is going to investigate it. I wish I was going along with him, because I would be more certain how the investigation is going to be conducted. I trust he will make a complete investigation that will either *clear Mr. Pelletier or put him where he belongs.

I do not know that any one has been dealt witli by this government, certainly not in my own department, in a harsh way for doing nothing more serious than what the hon. gentleman alleges has been done in this case. The hon. gentleman surely would not ask me to pronounce judgment upon a man before he has been heard in his own defence. If there be something wrong in the matter-and I confess that canvassing for a great public journal, if he is doing it in his own time, is not a very serious matter- but if he has been guilty of any partisanship, he will be dealt with. Parties have been dealt with who had shown violent partisanship in using the power of their office in order to induce people to vote in an election. In my opinion a civil servant should abstain from anything like partisanship. But the hon. gentleman will allow that he should be heard in his own defence, he will allow that I ought to ask the collector at Montreal what the circumstances were. In cases of people 'dismissed from my own department for political reasons, there was in every instance an investigation, and when the report came it was dealt with. The rule was not stretched in any case in order to inculpate any one. It was more pleasing to me to find that there were reasons that might justify the retention of the accused officer. Simply because a man had perhaps inadvertently taken part in an election, did not appear to be sufficient reason for dismissing him. There have been cases where complaints were made that men were writing for the papers, and even editing papers, which the department were able to overlook when all the circumstances were inquired into. However, I recognize the fact that the hon. gentleman wished to bring this matter before the House and the public, and as it appears that there is another *officer in another department against whom
a charge is made, we might pass this item, and the subject can be brought up again. 1 am fully impressed with this case, and I will look into it.

As relating to this subject, I may inform my hon. friend that a man in my own constituency, who was employed in the Department of Inland Revenue, was dismissed without investigation merely because he asked a question in a public meeting. I would consider that not a greater offence than canvassing for a public journal. It is desirable to have great public journals, of course, and those great journals can be conducted more economically if they are canvassed for by officers of the government. It is an advantage to the journal from its own standpoint, but from the standpoint of the public the arrangement might not be so advantageous as my hon. friend would seem inclined to regard it.

I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Customs to a matter which I may not have another opportunity of mentioning-a case in which the Bank of Nova Scotia was charged with the sum of $204 customs duty upon a safe which was made in Canada, exported to Newfoundland, and afterwards re-exported to Canada. The article was entirely of Canadian manufacture, but having been exported and having remained outside the country for a term exceeding three years, I think, upon its return to this country they were compelled to pay duty upon the whole of the original value. Possibly the minister has some remembrance of the case.

I do remember it. I think it was out of the country more than three years, and the tariff law which parliament passed, and which we only administer, says that if goods the manufacture or produce of Canada are exported to a foreign country and return unimpaired and unaltered within three years, they may come in free. In this case the safe was more than three years out of the country, and parliament has passed a law which takes away from us the power to admit such an article free. In this case there was no desire to deal in an exceptional manner. Any one could have appealed to the treasury board, and if the appeal had been reported favourably upon by them and adopted by council, the duty could have been remitted. But as I say, the department only administers the law, parliament makes the law.

In this ease it would appear that the safe which was in existence for a long time and which originally cost $680 was charged duty at the rate of 30 per cent upon the original value when it was_ returned to the country. It would appear as if it were a very extreme charge.
It was improved by the sea voyage.

1 do not suppose that safes are like ale or beer that is supposed to be improved by a sea voyage or even like port wine which I understand occasionally is improved by a sea voyage. The safe went out of the country by sea and came back in a few years. I would suppose that there must be some authority or power in the Department of Customs to deal with such a case. I have been asked to bring it to the notice of the hon. minister.

It could only be dealt with in the way I have pointed out. It is beyond the power of the department to do it. All the department could do would be to submit a case to the treasury board of the Privy Council.

I want a little more information. I am sorry to be bothering the hon. minister but he is laying down the principle, in so far as I under-stand it, that he does not think it any violation of the privileges of a member of the civil service in his department, a man being paid in a public department, a permanent officer like Mr. Pelletier, or any other man, to engage in the circulation of newspapers. The hon. gentleman has no objection to his doing so. Do I understand that to be the hon. minister's view of the matter ?
I said that I was reserving judgment, until I knew the whole facts of the case.

I do not ask the hon. minister to judge the man. I have no positive eviuence to produce before him. I recognize Mr. Pelletier's absolute right to be heard and to be dealt with most leniently, but providing that the hon. minister finds out that he has been employing himself in circulating the newspaper,* Le Canada,' I want to know whether the hon. minister thinks this is justifiable work ? In the hon. minister's department and throughout the country there are many political friends of my own and of others on this side of the House and if the hon. gentleman's friends have the right to circulate * Le Canada ' our friends have the right to circulate some other papers. We are paying taxes and the hon. minister will realize that. Although we are not in power, although we are a minority as far as this House is concerned, I think, we have still our rights of citizenship. Hon. gentlemen are going forth now to prepare for an election which is going to take place at a more or less early date. I can understand that the supporters of the government as they return from different parts of the country after having visited their constituents are not very urgent for an early appeal and of course ministers of the Crown must listen to those people as they return from the different parts of Canada, they will not have any very great encouragement to give 438J
them to have an early election. However, circumstances must govern ministers irrespective of their supporters. Although they may imagine that they are making a very wonderful impression on the country, if circumstances compel an appeal to the people they will find that they have not made any impression at all. These are the conditions which the cabinet must deal with. The work is to be done. The distribution of party newspapers and literature is of great assistance in the organization of a party and I think the hon. minister should now decide that principle. He does not condemn Mr. Pelletier. If he has not been doing that work he is not punished by the hon. minister and if the hon. minister decides that he m'ay do it he will not be punished. But, if lie may do it at all the other officers in his department may also do it.

I see that paper sometimes but I cannot read it as clearly as some others can. I judge that sometimes there are articles which favour the government but I do not wonder at that. But, to deal with the point that is put by the hon. gentleman, I think he is stretching the thing perhaps a little too far because he will remember that the Audit Act does not prohibit employees of the government from engaging in duties other than their own outside of office hours provided their salary is not over $1,000, and it is thus that you have civil servants outside of office hours engaging in the insurance business and in other kinds of work.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What salary does Mr. Pelletier draw ?

They are not prevented from doing that by the Audit Act, and therefore, if this gentleman were, upon his own time, engaging in something which was remunerative, it would have to be considered. I think the hon. gentleman is pressing the point rather far when he says that a man shall not, during his holidays, engage in any other work. If the hon. gentleman wants my opinion as to whether an officer, paid out of public money and during the time of his service to the country, should engage in other work which interferes with his duties, of course, there is only one answer-he should not do it.
The question of salary does not arise at all. I know what the Audit Act is. A permanent officer is always under pay whether he has a holiday or not. His salary is always going on.

He cannot get his holiday unless the collector gives him permission. It is provided for under the statute, but I suppose the collectors try to oblige their officers. I suppose if this officer went upon his holidays and engaged in doing some other work he did it with the view of earning something beyond his salary not in the time of the government.

I do not know tlie facts but I suppose this official, during liis holidays and upon his own time, lias been endeavouring to supplement his salary and he may have been canvassing for other papers at the same time. But, as I said, I do not know anything about that. I do not think we need uwell upon the matter any longer. I cannot say anything more than I have said.

I am sorry the hon. minister has not seen fit to lay down some guiding principle in this matter, not that I expect him to get on his feet again because as he says perhaps we have discussed it enough. I have not much confidence in any investigation he is going to make. He has thought of one hundred and one excuses for Mr. Pelletier by which lie can escape. He says that he may have been on his holidays and that he may have been canvassing for half a dozen papers. He should trot out one of these newspapers as evidence of the statement he makes. He has not, however, answered the question which I put to him.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if the Audit Act prevents a man after office hours from going to a public meeting and making a speech or asking a question ?
No, the Audit Act would not come in then.
Well then, why do you refer to it in connection with this gentleman ?
I was simply pointing out-

Yes, pointing out to evade the question. The hon. minister can not dismiss it with the bland smile which appears upon his countenance now. He never had that smile when he was in opposition ; he has assumed it since he got a big salary. I do not say that the Minister of Customs was particularly bad in dismissing Conservatives, and he may excuse himself because he has not been harsh, but he is part and parcel of the government that has been harsh, and he is responsible. I can tell him that the officials on the Murray canal were not accused of partisanship, but they were dismissed just because they voted Conservative in a gentlemanly fashion. I now want the few Conservatives who are left in the department to understand that they can go and canvass for ' La Patrie ' or any other Tory paper.
Hear, hear.

I had ' La Patrie ' in my mind, but perhaps it is not a Conservative paper, it is ' Le Journal ' I refer to. Is the principle laid down by the Minister of Customs that when a Conservative official is on his holidays, he can go and canvass for the ' Mail and Empire ' or any other Tory paper ?
No.
Do I understand that a Conservative official can canvass for the ' Mail and Empire,' and that he won't be dismissed ?
If a gentleman like the member for Compton should report to me, that an officer in the public service was out canvassing for the ' Mail and Empire,' I would say that I would inquire into the matter.
You would not dismiss him ?
It is very doubtful ; I have not dismissed many.

I was not present when the Minister of Customs gave an explanation with regard to the rights and immunities of public- officials, after office hours. Do I understand that it is permissible for officers in the civil service, who do not receive a salary in excess of $1,000, to canvass for insurance, for example, after office hours or before office hours, or during their holidays ? I had a complaint made by a business concern in Toronto during the present session, that an officer in the civil service. was canvassing their customers against them for certain goods. I made a complaint to the department, because I thought that such conduct was not justified by the law. It would seem rather extraordinary that officials should be permitted to engage in outside business under such circumstances.
I dare say the hon. gentleman knows the Act as well as I do.
I do not, that is why I ask the question.

It does not forbid an officer who is in receipt of less than $1,000 a year from engaging in some work that does not interfere with his duties. If he is in receipt of $1,000 or over, it does absolutely prohibit him.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What salary does Mr. Pelletier get 1
Five hundred dollars.
Why was Mr. James Currie, collector at Charlottetown, dismissed ?
He was superannuated.
Why ?

I do not remember, but I think it was on account of age.
Mi;. HACKETT. That can not be possible, because the very same day that Mr. Currie i was dismissed, a man of the same age was

appointed in St. John, N.B. What is the [DOT]explanation of that ? Why was Mr. Geo. Conroy, sub-collector at TIgnish dismissed ?
I have no recollection. When did that take place ?
It took place immediately after the Grit government came to power.
That was a long time ago.
It is only about seven years ago, and we all have occasion to remember it with i;egret.
I will look into the matter.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Was there an investigation in Mr. Conroy's case ?
No.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What did they dismiss him for ?

Simply because he was a Conservative.
Miscellaneous-amount required to pay for services of Thomas Kilroy, acting customs officer at Windsor. Ont., 360 days ending March 29, 1894, at $1.50 per day, $540.

Mr. Kilroy was employed as a temporary empolyee [DOT]at Windsor, prior to 1893, but at the close of that year his services were dispensed with, on the ground that the staff was sufficient without him. He was re-employed as temporary officer at that port during the months of March, February and April, 1893, by order of the then Controller of Customs, the Hon. N. C. Wallace. From the 1st of April, 1893, the collector of customs at Windsor was notified that Mr. Kilroy's services were to be discontinued, but it appears from an investigation made by Chief Inspector 5. W. MacMichael, that the then collector, Mr. Geo. E. Martin, did not notify him of the action of the department. The chief inspector's report which is dated 17th of October, 1900, clearly says that Mr. Kilroy was actually on duty at the port of Windsor for 360 days after the collector was notified of the discontinuance of his employment. This case was exactly similar to that of Mr. Jas. Gibson, who was employed at the port of Windsor at the same time, under the same circumstances. Mr. Gibson's case was provided for in the supplementary estimates, 1901-2, but Mr. Kilroy's claim could not be disposed of then for the reason that the late collector at Windsor had during the time Mr. Kilroy was without pay from the department, paid out of his own money $691.04 for groceries and supplies to Mr. Kilroy, [DOT]during the period covered by the claim.
Acting upon the advice of the Department of Justice, Mr. Kilroy, having made a petition of right to obtain payment for bis services, the Department of Customs refused to ask parliament for a vote to pay
the claim until such time as the late Mr. Martin's account had been properly adjusted. In the month of October, 1902, the executor of the estate of the late collector gave a release of all demands, discharging Mr. Kilroy from all claims; and on the same being submitted to the Department of Justice, they decided, in a letter of the 9th of May last, that the claim was one which the department might reasonably settle without reference to the courts.	These are the
circumstances of the case. The late collector sent word that he had dispensed witli the services of these two men. The collector never notified them, and they went on and rendered the services for the whole year, and claimed that having rendered the services they should be paid. Parliament paid Mr. Gibson's claim two years ago, and Mr. Kilroy's claim would have been dealt with at the same time, but the collector had advanced him so much out of his own pocket and the department would not pay his claim until a settlement had been made with the collector. In May last he brought a release from the executors to the Department of Justice.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Would it not have been fair to make the collector lose that money when he failed to give the notice ?
The poor man is dead now and the matter is settled. However, these officers rendered the services and they claim that they should be paid. The mistake was on the collector's part.
I wish to ask why Mr. John P. Brennan was dismissed from his position as sub-collector at Alberton ?
That is some years ago, and I cannot remember what the cause was. No doubt it was deemed sufficient at the time.

It is not very many years ago. I regret that the hon. minister is not able to give me an explanation. I think the people of our province are bound to resent the action of the government in cutting off the heads of the best men because they are Conservatives and placing inferior men in their places.

Have you a list of the gentlemen who are to be placed on the permanent staff ?

To pay provisional allowance at the rate ot $10 per month to Mr. J. W. T. Dixon of the dead letter office, Winnipeg, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act to the contrary, $120.

This officer is in Winnipeg and a provisional allowance is made to the officers of the department at Winnipeg. He is included in this. He is in the inside service but could not have the benefit of the provisional allowance except in this way. He has $400 per year. He was appointed temporary writer on the 1st of January, 1903, and was transferred to the Winnipeg dead letter office on the 13th of March. 1903. He was appointed to the inside service at Ottawa and was moved from Ottawa to Winnipeg.
Does the hon. gentleman not think that this sudden surprise will injure him ?	[DOT]

I think he will be able to stand it.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Could nobody he found in Winnipeg to fill that office ?	'	[DOT]

The Dead Letter Department is in the inside service. Until the last four or five years ail dead letter matter was dealt with at Ottawa, but by the legislation of 189S permission was granted to decentralize in order to save time, and dead letter branches of the main office at Ottawa were opened at Winnipeg and at other points remote from the centre here. But the officers appointed at the dead letter branch have always been men who have served here first and have become trained in the method.
To provide for eight additional junior second-class clerkships in the inside service, $5,800.

Some years ago third-class clerkships were abolished and a large number of clerks entered
Mr. LaRIVIERE.
the service as juniors in the capacity of temporary writers. Some sixty to seventy temporary clerks were appointed, some by the late and some by the present government, commencing at $400 and increasing at the rate of $30 per year. These are prizes which will be distributed wisely to those that-are deserving.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What salary' djo they start with ?
The junior second clerks start with $600 and the maximum is $1,000. Under the Civil Service Bill which passed to-day, they will enter at $700 and the maximum is $1,100.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
$5,800 would give the eight clerks $725 each.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. How many clerks are already employed in that office besides those six who are to be made permanent ?

The explanation of that $5,800 is this. There are some offices in connection with the international money-order branch who have a different status. It is intended to transfer them to the status of junior second class at the salary they now enjoy. There are five in that position and three new appointees at $600. The other five have gross salaries of $4,000. There are live transferred from one class to another and three new appointees. In fact this item is not large enough if the Civil Service Bill becomes law because the three new officers will begin at $700 and we are only providing for $600.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Were not these $4,000 voted in the main estimates ?

That might be, but it would not be applicable to them under a technical construction of the vote. Money voted for the payment of the salary of a man filling one position is not available for the payment of the salary of that person if put in another position. These five were formerly engaged as clerks in connection with the money exchange office at Montreal. We had to make an international exchange at Montreal on account of our business with the United States. But owing to some changes being made in connection with our international business, those men are to be made junior second class clerks at their present salary. The money voted to pay them in their former position would not be available to pay them now, because the money is not voted to pay the individual as such but as the occupant of the office.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman to fill the positions of those five ?
No, the offices are abolished.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: A junior second-class clerk lias been in the service for some time ; he started at $600, and iby statutory increases his salary has become $700 beginning on the 1st of July last. How will this Bill affect a junior second-class clerk who is in that position ?

It will not have any effect upon such officers, they will continue junior second-class clerks if they -reach $700, which is the minimum, and at the expiration of each year they will be eligible to another increase of $50. A second-class clerk who, at the time this Bill goes into operation, is in receipt of a salary not less than the minimum is not affected by the Bill, except that when he reaches $i,000, the present maximum, he will still be eligible to go on to the $1,100.

I have -been absent from the House for some time, and I am not conversant with the application of the Bill which has recently passed this House. I am interested in the welfare of the civil servants, and I would like to ask if by this Bill they will receive the annual increases which they were led to expect in joining the service ? In many instances civil servants have not received- these ircreases to the extent they were le-d to expect. I have in mind particularly some mail clerks who have served many years and who have not received their promotions from one class to another, nor the increases to which they are entitled. I would like to know if that would be remedied by this -Bill ?

My hon. friend says that he is particularly interested in the welfare of the civil servants, and yet lie was absent during the discussion of 'this Bill, which has now passed out of this House. I do not like to return to the discussion of a measure which has gone to the Senate. The Bill speaks for itself. I would remind the hon. gentleman that a measure which lias been passed through this House and become law this session deals with the status of railway mail clerks, and I do not think he will find one railway -mail clerk in Canada who will say he has been unjustly dealt with by the present government.

I am not speaking of the present government ; I think I can find mail clerks who think they have not had the promotion to which their length of service entitled them and which they anticipated when they joined the service.

The measure that passed in August last is of great advantage to the railway mail clerks of Canada, who have not hesitated to so express themselves. It has given them a much more satisfactory status than they ever before enjoyed, and they have expressed themselves to that effect in many ways to me.
How many officers of the service are eligible for promotion under this clause ?
There are sixty or seventy clerks who would be eligible. Others of these may -be appointed from time to time if the number of junior seconds had increased.
You are now appointing three ?

Yes. The hon. gentleman will remember that we have provided for the advancement of all these temporary clerks from the position they now occupy to be third-class clerks, and by the Bill which passed this House they can all be made third-class clerks, the minimum and maximum of which grade are $100 more than the minimum and maximum of the class to which they now belong.

Sixty or seventy are eligible for promotion to this junior second-class position, and- the minister is now taking a vote to provide for eight additional junior second-class clerks. He has explained that five officers will be taken from the exchange branch at Montreal. Then there will be only three vacancies while sixty or seventy are eligible ?
The POST-MASTER GENERAL. I told the hon. gentleman that it would be possible to appoint sixty or seventy. I suppose there are sixty or seventy temporary writers, and they have all passed a qualifying examination. I have stated that 1 trust that a liberal use will be made of the Bill which has passed this House in respect to these temporary writers. If that policy is adhered to, these temporary writers will receive a great advantage in being put into a class, the minimum and maximum of which are $100 more than that of the class to which they now belong.
To pay O. Higman for investigating the pneumatic tube service in the United States and reporting thereon, notwithstanding anything in the^Civil Service Act, $324.15.

The pneumatic tube service is a system that obtains in many cities of the United States for the rapid transmission of mail .matter to different places in the city. It has been tried for some years in New York, Washington, Philadelphia and majiy other cities, and I hope that 'in the not* distant f uture we will be able to adopt it in Canada. I sent Mr. Higman, who is an officer in. the Inland Revenue Department, to the United I States to examine and report upon this sys-I tern, and he made a very valuable report,
' which will be useful when we come to conI si-der the question of adopting the system to the Canadian post office.
Does the government expect to confer any advantage on the public by the adoption of that system ?

Nothing has been decided. The first step is to study the system and to consider whether it is applicable to Canada. I think that the report is a very valuable one. I have given some study to it, and I think that it might _ be usefully adopted for distributing mail matter in large cities. It affords a very excellent method of rapid delivery.

I suppose in a city like Montreal you would have a central office from which you would distribute the mail matter by this system. It does not mean that you are going to run a tube into every man's house.

The pneumatic tube system is this : You have underground steel pipes, perhaps 8 inches in diameter. In the United States they have [DOT]three different sizes of 8, 10 and 12 inches in diameter. Then there is what is called a carrier which travels inside this tube, a cartridge shaped structure, perhaps 30 inches long, and as large as the tube will allow. This is filled with mail matter, closed up, and forced by pneumatic pressure from one place* to another connected by the tube. The mail matter distributed by that system starts from the 'post office or from some central point, and thence is distributed throughout the city wherever the system reaches. Where the public thoroughfares are thronged with traffic which occasions delay in the transmission of mail matter by vehicles, this system is found to afford very rapid delivery.
It only carries mail matter from the central office to branch offices ?
Yes.
It does not interfere with the ordinary mail carriers or distributors ?
It would not affect letter-carriers.
Over how great a distance would this pneumatic system be feasible 1

I am afraid it would not go under the Straits. I think it would carry two or three miles. If you renewed the power at different points you might send it an indefinite distance, but I do not know how you would continue the pressure.
Is this the total cost of the investigation ?
Yes.
What is the cost per mile?

I cannot say from memory. The cost of installation involves more than merely putting the pipe under ground. You have to have an engine, for instance, and in a large city like Toronto that would involve the acquisition of a site for operations, where you would need to build a station and an engine house. Then at other points there would need to be some more machinery.
To increase the salary of F. H. Smith, first-class clerk, to $1,750 from 1st July, 1903, and arrears from 1st July, 1901, notwithstanding anything in the -Civil Service Act, $150.

Mr. Smith was formerly assistant inspector at the Soo. He was transferred to the inside service on his former salary as an inspector. I think he was at the maximum of his class of assistant inspector. After a year or so it was suggested that he should be given a different status, and I made him a first-class clerk, and proposed to treat him as a first-class clerk from the time of his transfer, and that is the reason we are giving him tills small increase. He is a very worthy officer indeed. He is a son of the late Postmaster General the Hon. Sydney Smith.
To provide for the appointment of an assistant post office inspector in the Vancouver division, $1,500.

That sum is to provide for the payment of Mr. [DOT]T. R. N. Greenfield as first-class clerk, having a salary at the present time of $1,500 a year. He was appointed to the inside service here on the 1st of July, 1883. He was transferred to the post office inspector's office, Victoria, on the Gth of July, 1893. Formerly there was only one inspector for the province of British Columbia, stationed on the island at Victoria. That was found inconvenient, and I laid the foundation for the creation of another inspectorate at the city of Vancouver' upon the mainland, and appointed Mr. Dormer to the office after he had been tried a while as to his qualifications. For a time he continued in Vancouver as first-class clerk, conducting his office as a branch of the Victoria office. He has been in the service for many years, he is thoroughly efficient and highly recommended as being well qualified for the position of an assistant inspector.
Have you only one inspector there ?
Only one on the mainland.
How many assistants ?
This is the only assistant the inspector has in his office.
