Before this item is declared carried, I would like to ask the hon. minister if he has heard from Prince Edward Island in regard to the illness of the Hon. Mr. Breeken, who is inspector there ?

Yes, I am extremely sorry to say that it is worse than a case of illness. Mr. Breeken died this morning. At least I received a despatch early this morning announcing his death. Mr. Breeken was at one time a member of this House, and there are some present who will remember him. I am sure they have a very kindly recollection of him. He proved himself an admirable officer, faithful and efficient, and the country has lost a capable officer in the death of Mr. Breeken.
To provide for Increases of $50 each to fourth-class clerks recently promoted from the class of stampers and sorters, such increases to date from the times when they would respectively become entitled to Increases if they had remained in their former class, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act to the contrary, $3,950.

Before we proceed with this item, as I see we are approaching the close of the supplementary estimates, if there is not another leaf to be attached which is not already down-possibly there may be-I would like to bring a question to the attention of the lion. Postmaster General in connection with certain reports which have come to me, I think fairly well-founded, that a Mr. Latour who was Postmaster in tlie Public Works Department in Ottawa, owing to ill-health, has received six months leave of absence. Is that correct ?
I really do not know.

And that he has been replaced by his son, which is a matter of indifference to me. Whether he has been replaced by his son or by the son of some other son, does not make any particular difference to me. But, I understand that this gentleman has had a six months leave of absence. I suppose that would imply that his salary is continued ?
I made some inquiry in my department, and I find we never had an officer of that name in the department.
He is postmaster of the Public Works Department.
I have not inquired throughout the service, but we never had an officer of that name in the Post Office Department. Thou canst not shake thy gory locks at me. Thou canst not say I did it.
I suppose that when a man was a postmaster he was connected with the postal' service.
No, we have no such officer.
Do you mean to say that I will have to turn my attention to the hon. Minister of Public Works ?

I heard the hon. gentleman say before six o'clock that he thought this officer was in my department and my hon. friend the hon. Minister of Customs desired to transfer the discussion to me. I made inquiry in the department, and I find that we have no such officer.

I am making the usual effort of gentlemen who are dealing with the government, and they are shifting from one position to another. The hon. Minister of Customs, the head of the collecting department of this government, this afternoon referred me to the hon. Postmaster General. But, of course, he did not know what he was talking about. I thought he did not know this afternoon.
You should not let him escape.

I did not like to let him escape- but he assured me he was not smiling and consequently I considered he might be serious when he said that when the hon. Postmaster General's estimates came up, I would have an opportunity of discussing the matter. However, the question I have to raise is that a public officer of the government has been granted leave of absence and is now in the employ of ' Le Canada,' newspaper, which is the leading Liberal organ in Quebec, and is travelling through that province being the head agent of that Liberal organ, seeking subscriptions for it. More than that, he is going about through the various post offices which do come under, I presume, the hon. Postmaster General. We find that he goes to the postmasters where he thinks he can frighten and control them and asks them to furnish him with a list of people who receive at these offices papers that are favourable in their editorial departments to the opposition members of this House.
Does the Postmaster General think it right that any government official should be guilty of such conduct ? I have this information from a source which I do not feel at liberty to use, but it is a source from which the Postmaster General has no doubt got information, and I think he would acknowledge it as a reliable source. I do not think that the Postmaster General would take the same view, outside the cabinet of course, as his colleague the Minister of Customs, who stated this afternoon that it was not partisan work to disseminate the seeds of Liberalism by canvassing for a Liberal party organ. I look upon it as partisanship of the highest order, for there is nothing which can so much redound to the benefit of a political party as that the faithful should read daily the organ of that party. Seven years ago the Prime Minister decided that any official guilty of partisan conduct should leave the service. What is be going to do with Mr. Latour ? I am informed Mr. POPE.
that he is .postmaster of the Public Works Department.
He cannot be postmaster of the Public Works ; they have no postmaster.

That is his description. Of course, in the country parts our information may not be absolutely correct about these officers. They may come down and boast amongst us in order to make themselves out great men amongst the ignorant agricultural community, so that their partisan works may bear greater fruit than if they came down simply under their own name,, without such a high-sounding description. But that is the way Mr. Latour represents himself in the country parts, and he is represented as having been replaced by his son, at a salary of $1,200 a year, and he is cut loose on the province of Quebec to spread ' Le Canada.'

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: On sick leave.

When my hon. friend was discussing the estimates of the Minister of Customs this afternoon, I was not giving very great attention to the discussion ; but when I heard it stated that this man was an officer of the Post Office Department; I was not in a position either to affirm it or deny it; and when the House rose at six o'clock, I asked the officers of my department if there was such an officer, because if there had been, it would have been my duty to have looked into the case. I did not learn until eight o'clock that there was no such officer in the Post Office Department. In whatever branch of the service he is employed, my hon. friend says that he has been applying to the postmasters throughout this country for the names of subscribers to newspapers. My opinion is that the names of the addresses of mail matter, newspapers, and all other kinds, is confidential information, which no postmaster is warranted in revealing to any person. No postmaster will be allowed to do that with impunity, so long as I have anything to say in the matter ; and if the hon. gentleman is aware of any postmaster having so far forgotten his duty as to disclose to any one the names on newspapers, or any other mail matter, without the authority of the addressees, it will be my duty to call that postmaster to account. If my hon. friend will furnish me with that information, I will at once proceed on the line I have mentioned. But it
would be rather unfair to ask me to proceed to discipline or to find out who may have transgressed, among the large number of postmasters. I am sure my hon. friend would not ask that. I do not know what department the official is in.
I would ask the Minister of Finance if there is not a man named Latour in the service of the government in Prince Edward Island ?

I have made inquiries with regard to a man named Latour. There is no postmaster in the Public Works Department that I know of, but there was a man named Latour in the temporary employ of the department. He has not been in the employ of the department for some considerable time.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
On sick leave perhaps.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS No, he is not drawing any pay from the department. This may be the man who is canvassing. I agree with my hon. friend the Postmaster General, that if he were in the employ of the government in any way, his conduct would be quite irregular and improper.
What salary was he getting.
Two dollars a day. I think. That is all the information I can give.
I think that is the bird we are after.

I have no proof with regard to the conduct of Mr. Latour ; but I can assure you that during the election of 1900 he was very active in the county of Prince, in the province of Prince Edward Island. When the judge of the county court called in, under the authority of the law, the ballot boxes from the different polling divisions, one was missing, and we alleged, and can substantiate the fact, that this Mr. Latour was the means of getting that ballot box out of the way. I tell you further that if this Mr. Latour places a foot on the soil of the iwovince of Prince Edward Island, he will find himself in a very hot box.	*

The hon. member for Compton (Mr. Pope), in discussing some of the other items of. the Post Office Department. asked if any provision was being made in these estimates to pay the men who were deprived of their statutory increases for two or three years, the sums they were then deprived of ?

The hon. gentleman presents the question as if what were known as statutory increases were legal liabilities of the Crown to those officers. That is an erroneous view to take. It is discretionary with the government to pay these statutory increases or not. Therefore it cannot be said that if a man does

not get the statutory increase, lie has anything coming to him, or there can be any arrears owing to him.	,

We have often considered this matter in this House. We are not wrong in assuming that these people are [DOT]entitled to a certain annual increase, according to the statutory arrangement of the department or the government. A man [DOT]commences at $400, and he is entitled to an increase of $50 a year. It is plain that he is entitled to it, or you could not give it to him. The particular man is not named, hut the inducement is held out to every young man who enters the service and who is worthy of being kept there. If he is not worthy of being kept there, dismiss him. But if he is an efficient officer, he is entitled to his increase. Were he in the employ of a private corporation or individual and did not get the increase to which he was entitled, he would go on strike and the Minister of Labour and the deputy would go down to see whether they could not induce his employer to give him the extra $50 or $60 which he had earned. When we have a Minister of Labour in the government itself, he ought to be able to exercise on the cabinet that authority which he sometimes *exercises in private matters. The ministers tell us that it is not they but the deputy heads who select - those they consider deserving of an increase. No doubt if we had the deputy heads here, they would shift the responsibility on to the chief clerks. It is very difficult to believe that in the selection, politics rather than merit have not an influence. It would be a great relief to members of parliament if our civil service were put into the hands of a commission, as it is done in England, and thus remove all opportunity for the exercise of political favouritism. That would be better for the public life of Canada and we would have more even handed justice dealt all around.

Some weeks ago I asked the Postmaster General Why the postmaster at the village of Enterprise was dismissed. This man kept his office in good condition, took no part in politics, and gave general satisfaction, and it is difficult to understand why lie should be dismissed and another man put in his place. The postmaster at Enterprise was dismissed on account of his mismanagement of the office. He was charged, among other things, with sending out his own business letters through the post unpaid.

Under this item I would like to make a remark with regard to one class that do not seem to have received any attention. The letter-carriers, the mail clerks, the accounting postmasters and town postmasters have all been assisted, their salaries have all been increased, and I am sure that during this growing time we all appreciate that fact. But a large majority of the postmasters, the men who render the best service for the smallest amount of money, the country postmasters, have received no increase whatever. I do not know how it is in the east, but in the western country they generally get from $12 to $50 a year. When a man or some member of his family has to stay at home for half a day to attend to one post office, and to keep it open for the convenience of the public, it becomes a hardship when labour is so expensive as it is during the summer months in our country. In the county I have the honour to represent I think there are from six to ten post offices that have been closed this year because the Postmaster General cannot get any one to accept them at the miserable salary offered. I spoke upon this subject last year, and I said that if the Postmaster General could not bring down * some systematic measure to give these country postmasters more salary, in the new districts their salaries should be charged up to the immigration fund. One of the greatest drawbacks of keeping immigrants in the country is the want of postal facilities, next to schools. Last year I cited a case 28 miles. from Swan river, in the Thunder Hill district, where a family had come from the north of Ireland with eleven children. They had neither school nor post office. Finally he wrote me saying that he would leave and go back home within three months unless he got some place where he could educate his children, and get some postal facilities. He was able to get a school, but a post office has only recently been established. That is a sample case of a good many others.
The hon. gentleman knows of no case where a post office recommended by the inspector in Manitoba or the territories has not been opened.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, I did not say it had not been opened, I said a post office had been opened now in the place I mentioned. That is not in my county, and it was when I was commissioner of immigration that the post office was opened. But I am explaining that the postmasters do not get sufficient salary to pay them for keeping the post offices open. There ought to be a minimum salary of $40 or $50 a year assured before a post office is established. I do not contend that the postal system should be a revenue producing branch of the department. I believe that the public convenience should be considered first, and then if it is afterwards self-supporting, well and good. I submit that the hon. minister, who always takes an interest in seeing that people are properly paid for their services, might seriously consider whether some new means cannot be devised by which, if a rural system cannot be made practicable, the country postmaster shall be paid for his services in a better manner than he is at the present time.

I should say that there was no postal note system In 1896. The postal note system lias since been established, and it lias proved a very ready and cheap means for the transmission of sums of money up to $10. Thus far I have given the committee the increases. I have to break in upon this line of argument, and I now take up another biancli, not dealing with increases. For many years prior to the 30th June, 1896, the revenue of the Post Office Department failed yearly to meet the expenditure by very large sums, and for the fiscal year ending 30th June, 1896, the revenue of the department fell short by $781,142.19 of meeting the expenditure. There was a. loss on the working of the department for that year of over three-quarters of a million dollars. As hon. gentlemen will remember, in 1898-9 there was a very material reduction in the revenue of the department caused by the reduction of the letter rates, both Canadian and imperial. On Christmas Day, 1898, the letter rate from Canada to the United Kingdom fell from 5 cents to 2 cents. Subsequently the same reduction took place on all letters from Canada to various parts of the empire, and to-day 2 cents takes a letter from Canada to every part of the British empire. That reduction in the rate of from 5 to 2 cents seemed to indicate a loss, unless followed1 by an increased volume of business, of a considerable amount of revenue. It will be recalled that on the 1st January, 1899, the rate on domestic letters was reduced from 3 cents to 2 cents per ounce. On the same day we reduced the rate on letters from Canada to the United States from 3 cents to 2 cents per ounce. It is impossible to tell definitely what effect these great reductions have had upon the revenue of the department, but the late Minister of Finance, in speaking in the House a year or so before 1896, indicated that a very considerable loss of revenue would follow from a reduction of the domestic letter rate. The late leader of the opposition, Sir Charles Tupper, placed that amount of $1,000,000. The late Minister -of Finance, Mr. Foster, I think, placed it
in the vicinity of a million dollars. Whab ever view you may attach to the effect of the reduction, it certainly is a fact that so far as it goes it leaves in the pockets of the people the percentage of the postage which they otherwise would have had to pay had they transmitted through the post office the volume of letters which! we have carried since this reduction went into force. It is not unreasonable to say that these reductions have left in the pockets of the people at least $1,000,000.
We had a balancing up for the fiscal year ending June 30th, 1902, and the result was that for that year, the revenue met all the expenditure of the department, with the exception of the cost of operating in the Yukon, and left us a surplus of $5,109.14.
What was the deficit in the Yukon ?

I do not remember it for that year, but I will give it to you for this year in a moment. The reason I omitted the Yukon service in the public accounts up to the present, has been, in order that it might be possible to institute a comparison. There was no Yukon mail service prior to the present government assuming office, and therefore we could not compare it with anything which had gone before. Taking the year that has just closed, I will give the figures both including the Yukon and excluding the Yukon, so that hon. gentlemen may draw their own deductions. There will always be a deficit in the post office service of the Yukon because they must have the same rate of postage in the Yukon as in the other parts of Canada, while there is no prospect of the cost of labour there coming down to the level of cost of labour in older Canada- there may be approaches to equalization, but that will be in the distant future. If we had had no Yukon expenditure and no Yukon deficit to pay, the working of the department this year would have resulted in our having a surplus of $395,316.31.
Hear, hear.
Omitting the deficit in the Yukon, I say that the Post Ottice Department to-day hands over to the treasury of Canada 5395,316.31 for the year's work.
What was the deficit in the Yukon ?

The deficit in the Yukon was $102,614.31, and paying the deficit in the Yukon, and paying all the expenditure of the post office service in every part of Canada, and including and charging against us the deficit in the Yukon, we have to-day a net surplus of $292,702.23. of revenue over expenditure for the year ending June 30, 1903.
Hear, hear.

For the year ending the 30tli of June, 1896, we had a loss of $781,162.19, and we have wiped out all that loss and we have today a surplus over and above our expenditure, amounting to over three quarters of a million dollars; and the people have in their pockets a million of dollars or so each year, in reduced rates which I presume they would not have had if the higher- rates were charged.
Hear, hear.

But leaving aside the reduction of rates, then so far as the taxpayers of Canada are concerned, there is a change from a deficit of $781,152.19 in 1896, to a surplus of $292,702.23, which means a total change in the accounts of $1,073,854.42.

The minister will not pretend to say that was all from revenue of the Post Office Department, because the money we voted a few years ago to wipe out that $700,000 did not come from the post office at all.
The hon. gentleman evidently thinks that that $781,000 is a cumulative deficit.
Yes.

Then he is entirely in error. The sum of $781,152.09 is the result of the operation simply of the one fiscal year ending the 30th June, 1896, taking all the revenue collected for that year and making the expenditure for that year within these twelve mouths only. There was a complete commencement and closing of accounts for that year, and to carry on the service for that fiscal year, without any part of any other year, and without any balance from any prior year, for that one year of 365 days, it cost Canada $781,152.09, more than the gross revenue, to carry on the service.
For this past year, we have paid the whole expenditure for the service from the first to the end of the year, and Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
have on hand a surplus, excluding the Yukon, of $395,316, and paying the deficit of the Yukon we have a surplus of $292,702, It means a change from the deficit to the surplus in the ledgers of Canada, amounting for the year to a betterment of $1,073,854.42 since 1896.
Hear, hear.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I am asked, what it is proposed to do with this fund. I agree with hon. gentlemen that in a country like Canada we should -not treat the post office service as a money making service. If it can be made to take care of itself, that I think would be satisfactory to the people of Canada, and it is but right that those who are engaged in the carrying on of the service, should, when circumstances will warrant it, be remembered. It is in view of that fact and in view of what seems to me to be the satisfactory position of the department, that I have been able of late to propose to parliament-and which parliament has been good enough to give effect to-recommendations having in view increases of salary to those in the service. Legislation has been passed during last year and this year, improving the salaries here and there. I shall not enumerate what has been done in that respect, as it is within the knowledge of hon. gentlemen. But my hon. friend from Provencher (Mr. Lariviere) and my hon. friends on this side of the House, have from time to time been pressing the department to consider the position of the country postmasters. I would be only too pleased if I were able to consider these gentlemen even more favourably than I now can, but so far as the present is concerned. I will give you the conclusion at which I have arrived. There are many postmasters throughout Canada whose offices may serve ten, or a dozen, or twenty immediate neighbours, and these postmasters are only paid a nominal sum for the trouble of keeping the office. That scale of payment did not originate with the present administration, and I am not aware that it originated with the prior administration, nor does it make any difference. It has been acquiesced in by both parties, and without any blame to either side. The exigencies of the country, our sparse population compared with our vast area, made it necessary to adopt some means to give postal facilities, and thus this system grew up in our broad Dominion. The question is, how can it be bettered ? At present, where the revenue is merely nominal, amounting to perhaps $10 or $20 a year, it has been the practice to pay postmasters a minimum fee of $10, going up to $12 or $15. I propose that from the first of July last all this class shall receive a minimum fee of $25.
A petition was presented to me last spring on behalf of a certain other class of postmasters, called accounting postmasters, ask-

ing for increases of pay and allowances. They asked that these allowances and increases should be made applicable to the territories and Manitoba. There is a great difficulty always in discriminating between one class and another, one locality and, another; and if what they asked for were granted, not merely to those in the western country, but to the same class in all Canada, it would involve increased expenditure exceeding $1,000,000 a year. I therefore shrank from meeting such a large demand. The system at present in Canada, which has been handed down to all succeeding governments ever since we have had a post office in Canada, and from pre-confederation days, has been to pay the postmasters a salary based upon the revenue of the office. There are a few exceptions to this scheme ; but most of the postmasters of Canada to-day are being remunerated on the basis of the old system which has prevailed for so many years, namely, a percentage of the revenue. With regard to them, I propose to increase their remuneration by 10 per cent of the amounts that they would derive according to the existing scale, that 10 per cent to be paid to them, not only in respect of their salaries, but in respect of what are known as their forward allowances, which form a considerable item in the gross expenditures of the Post Office Department. These increases will make a substantial inroad upon the revenue of the department. Added to these the increases in salaries which are authorized by legislation will make a much greater demand upon the treasury. But I have no doubt that we shall be able to meet them successfully, and I trust without having to face parliament with the statement that the department, even for the current year, has been administered at a loss.
In referring to the organization and development of the department, I omitted to say that a little more than a year ago the department opened negotiations with the United States for the purpose of simplifying the money order system between Canada and that country, enabling the Canadian people to remit small sums of money through the post office to a very much larger number of places throughout the United States than the former arrangements made possible. Those negotiations were successful, and an international arrangement was made by which the number of money-order offices in the United States upon which we might remit was greatly increased. The actual increase amounts to over 28,000. Up to the time I speak of, we could only send money-orders payable, in the United States at. something like 5.900 post offices ; but by the arrangement made, which was mutual, we are now able, for the convenience of the Canadian people, to remit money to no less than 34.000 post offices in the United States. A corresponding convenience is afforded to the people of the United States in remitting to Canada. The 439
practical working of this, so far as the volume of business goes, is as follows. This system has been in force now two clear years. For the year prior to its going into force the total number of money-orders remitted by Canada to the United States was 204,053 for sums of money aggregating $2,11S,295.33. For the year just closed the number of money-orders sent by Canada to the United States was 344,605, representing in money $3,682,189.96, being an increase of 72 per cent. The United States, in like manner, have remitted to Canada a much larger sum through the post office than under the former system. The figures of the return business are as follows : For the last year under the old system the number of money-orders sent from the United States to Canada through the post office in 1901 was 137,611, representing the sum of $1,909,168.74, and the amount of the year ending the 30th of June, 1903, was 270,779, representing in money $3,783,925, or an increase of 98 per cent.
The department has had negotiations with the United Kingdom for an extension of our money-order system on the same basis with that part of the empire, but up to the present time we have not been able to make that arrangement. We have also extended that system lately to Newfoundland, and| we have negotiations for its extension to many other parts of the empire and other countries. For example, negotiations are on foot at the present time to extend it to Bermuda, Barbadoes, Jamaica, the Leeward Islands, Tobique and British Guiana. We have also during the year completed arrangements for the extension of our money-order system to Norway, the Transvaal, Cape Colony and Trinidad ; and negotiations are pending with Austria-Hungary and Sweden. These are all conveniences to the Canadian people for the transmission of small sums of money to the various parts of the world. I might also say that at the postal convention, held in London last July, the following resolution, on the motion of Canada, was adopted :
That it is advisable to adopt the principle of cheap postage between the different parts of the British empire on all newspapers, and periodicals published therein, and the Prime Minister desires to draw the attention of His Maiesty's government to the question of reduction in the outgoing rate. They consider that each government should be allowed to determine the amount to which they may reduce such rates and the time for such reduction going into effect.
Acting upon this resolution, the Canadian Post Office Department put itself in early communication with various parts of the empire in order to obtain permission for the public in Canada to forward their newspapers and periodicals to all parts of the empire at the domestic letter rate, and already that permission has been granted in respect of the following countries : The United Kingdom, Balia-



mas, the Barbadoes, Bermuda. British Honduras, Cyprus, Ceylon, Falkland Islands, Cambia, Hong Kong, Leeward Islands (including Antigua, &c.), New Zealand, Transvaal, Sarawak, Sierra Leone, Turk's Island and Zanzibar. To all those countries to-day Canadian publications pass at the same rates as are charged for their transmission throughout Canada itself. And considering the very cheap rate of transmission of newspapers, periodicals and other Canadian publications throughout our own country, I think it may be said that no country in the world enjoys to-day as cheap a rate for the transmission of its publications, dealing with our own life, giving people outside of our country the. knowledge of our affairs, as does Canada.
Are there not some corresponding increases ? Has not the rate on parcels been increased and city deliveries?

There was an increase in some of the parcel post regulations. In 1897 there was a rate imposed upon newspapers of a half a cent a pound, but even that rate has been almost cut in two by legislation this session. The legislation of this session has reduced the newspaper rate from half a cent per pound to one-quarter cent a pound on all newspapers to he carried 300 miles.

So far as the accounting postmasters are concerned, to which reference has been made by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. LnRivi&re), he has said that a man who has been receiving $40 a year, under this arrangement will receive $4 a year more. That is true, but a postmaster who has been receiving a salary of $1,000 a year will receive an increase of $100 a year.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. But that does not affect a $40 affair.
Mr. HUGHES (King's, P.E.I.) It must be a small office indeed where the salary is 439}
not more than $40.
