I am sure the people of this country will congratulate the Postmaster General upon his management of that de partment for the last seven years.

I think it is unfortunate that the hon. gentleman from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hughes) should throw this note of discord into a happy family such as we are at this moment. I say it is unfortunate, because it makes me angry when I hear a man making false claims. Now, the Postmaster General made no claim to being a party to this prosperity in that particular, and I think _he was wise. I think he followed the example of the young man we read of the other day in England, the young Marquis of Salisbury, who inherited his father's magnificent estate. Some American correspondent called upon him, and looked over this magnificent pile of buildings erected by his ancestors two or three hundred years ago, the old Cecils, who had won it for the modern Salisburys, who for the last 30 or 40 years had never put a brick to the castle or added an acre to the estate. But the Yankee blusterer commenced to congratulate the young man upon being the owner of this great estate. The fellow was abashed by the candour of the young man, who sat there clothed with humility and sorrow, and who replied : ' I am ashamed to inherit this magnificent estate, in building up which I have done nothing ; it is the work of the great Cecils of two or three hundred years ago.' The Yankee blusterer turned away, he had met an honest and noble-minded man, such as are many of the better classes in England. Now, I think the Postmaster General-or shall we call him the Minister of Labour ? Which title does the hon. gentleman prefer ? I do not know what to call him. I do not wish to hurt bis feelings, because he may have a preference for one title over the other. I think he should be called the Postmaster General and not the Minister of Labour, because bis ample proportions do not fulfil the poetical idea of a Minister of Labour. I think a Minister of Labour should be thin and lank, and show the evidences of a laborious life. He should be lean and hungry-looking like Cassius, rather than the robust gentleman he is, who seems to have been reared in the lap of luxury and to have lived there all his life. However, apart from that, I hope the Postmaster General is too modest to accept all this honour that has been thrust upon him by the hon. member for Prince Edward Island.

I am proud on belialf of Canada to see this splendid showing, to know that our post office pays. I assume that our post office pays $202,000 of surplus into the treasury of Canada. I understand from the hon. Postmaster General that we pay all the bills In connection with the post office for Canada and for the Yukon, and that we have then $292,000 to pay into the treasury of Canada. If that is the statement it is a creditable showing for Canada, but it is only what might have 'been expected. There never was a country the foundation of whose administration in every department of government was laid with such wisdom as that of the administration of Canada as laid in 1867 and from that time down to 1896. These hon. gentlemen have inherited one of the most perfect systems of government that was ever developed in the British world. All the great public works had been built. The post office system had been extended all through Canada, and these hon. gentlemen had only to sit down and see the revenues flow in. They had not to turn their hand in any department to help Canada, and until this scheme bf the transcontinental railway was brought forth they never had added one thing to the public life of Canada or secured one dollar of revenue for Canada. They have been heirs to a magnificent estate, and I have never heard these hon. gentlemen in the course of this parliament attempt to claim credit for the great progress that Canada has made. They do not deserve it, and I will appeal to any hon. gentleman in this House to say whether in justice and fair-play, apart from political partisanship, he can wake any claim for this government, except that they had the luck to inherit a magnificent estate, at a very fortunate time, when the great public works had been constructed and when we had been waiting for the development which was bound to come in consequence of these great public works. We had settled the principles of government, we had constructed the great public works, and we had said to the people of Canada : Wait, the Intercolonial Railway, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the canals cannot produce this great wealth and progress in a day. We said that this development would come. It came in due time, and it came when the great public men of Canada had pointed out that it should come. In the vicissitudes of fortune these lion, gentlemen opposite came into power and inherited the results of the splendid achievements of others. I was glad that the hon. Postmaster General did not make any claim to the credit for any of these great results. I always say in the country, of course, that Canada is prosperous and that Canada must become a great nation, because the party that had been in power for eighteen years had laid well and truly the foundations of national greatness. It was at the time that they had completed

the work that these hon. gentlemen came into power. After they had been criticising the Conservative party for eighteen years, they came into power and they paid a splendid tribute to our policy by adopting it, because, as sensible men, they could do nothing else, although I believe there were some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House who would have been reckless enough to have adopted some other policy had not public opinion been so strong. While I congratulate hon. gentlemen opposite on the progress that Canada is making, I would say that it is only the progress that I have been predicting for the last twenty years. I used to say : Wait, this country will be great; wait, the people's railway will pay an enormous revenue ; wait, immigration will pour in ; wait until we break down the prejudice against Canada ; wait until we get the Liberal party to cease reviling and slandering Canada, and then her wealth will be increased. Whenever I made the declaration that this progress would come, the Grit party were howling that Canada would be broken. The right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) was reviling us down below, describing us as the shreds and patches of Canada and insulting every portion of Canada. I have no doubt this progress would have come years ago if, when our Finance Minister went to England a few years ago to float a loan, he had not been met by the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce and by the financial papers which the right hon. gentleman controlled, in an attempt to break down the credit of Canada by one of the meanest, the lowest political conspiracies that ever disgraced any country. Even in war there are honourable principles. A man must fight fairly even in war, if he is to be regarded as a generous and decent foe, and those same principles must be applied to political warfare. The Conservative party stood up for eighteen years and fought for Canada just as much as if a foe had invaded Canada, because the Liberal party were just as much an invading army as if Canada had been invaded by Americans or Mexicans. That was what always angered me. I have always taken the view that I have no right to oppose my political opponents by saying one word which will hurt Canada. If I differ with the party or the policy of lion, gentlemen opposite I will attack them as vigorously as I can, but I will never say a word against my country. It is my bound-en duty, as a citizen of Canada, to say words of praise for my country or to hold my tongue. No man in this opposition, the only loyal opposition that ever stood out in defence of the whole country, in all the debate on the transcontinental railway, has uttered a word except in praise of Canada. Yet, when hon. gentlemen opposite were opposing the great Canadian Pacific Railway, the country rang with slander from

end to end, until no man believed himself safe to live in this country for twenty-four hours. The lion. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson), with that sweet, low voice of liis, charmed the people of Ontario with the most reckless slanders against the people of Canada that were ever uttered by any public man. There never was an occasion on which a more reckless stream of slander was wer poured from any human throat than that which flowed in a continuous stream from the lion. Minister of Customs. That party kept back the progress of Canada for twenty years by this continuous flow of slander. It is bad enough to see these men occupying the treasury benches. It is the Irony of fate that the Conservative party should sit here after we have made this country, and see hon. gentlemen opposite occupying the treasury benches. They wear the robes that they never won ; they wear the chaplet to which they are not entitled. They never won the race, and yet they want the bay. They want the plume, and yet they never won the race. The Conservative party have always been anxious for the success of Canada. We want to see this country great. I feel that I want to be a Canadian in any part of the world. The old Roman used to say in every part of the world : ' Civis Romanus sum.' I want the magic wrds ' Civis Canadensis Sum ' to be more attractive even than the old boast of the Roman. I can sit here at any time and see these hon. gentlemen go along with their estimates. I can help them to vote their estimates, until they claim that this progress is due to their party or to their policy. I commend the hon. gentleman for his modesty to-uight, because I remember that in the' earlier part of this session, when he was making a speech in regard to post office affairs, he took occasion to rake up some old matters that had better have been left alone at the present time. I noticed a change in his manner to-night, and I was delighted to see that he is improving. The improvement mav not be very marked, but in him it is worthy of commendation. On this occasion the hon. Postmaster General has absolutely disclaimed any connection with the result which he has been able to show. So he says : I have had nothing to do with this, I am only a little pipe through which the water is running, and I take no credit for it. I have no fault to find, and I say it is a creditable showing on behalf of Canada. If hon. gentlemen opposite take that position, I have no fault to find, but whenever the Liberal partv of Canada attempts to claim one iota of credit for the development of this country, they make a false claim, and they must be accused of false pretenses.

I understood from the Postmaster General that the minimum increase granted to postmasters would be $25. Now. if a postmaster receives $40 a year, would he get $65 now, or would he only get
10 per cent on the $40, which would make his salary $44.

I stated that a large number of postmasters in Canada now receive salaries amounting from $10 to $20 per year, and in future the minimum salary of these gentlemen will be $25. As to the postmasters who are paid by commission, they will hereafter receive an increase of 10 per cent on that commission, be their salaries small or large. On the revenue of the office they will receive 10 per cent more than they formerly received.

I have sat in the House for some days listening to the increased votes which have been granted to the various departments, and in the interest of my constituents, I often felt like making a strenuous protest. If the Postmaster General, who had charge of the Bill granting increases to civil servants, and if many of his supporters were on this side of the House, I can imagine what protests they would have made in the interests of the farmers who in the days of adversity, they professed such an affection for. However that may be, let me point out that the country postmasters receive under this proposal the smallest increase of any of the civil servants whose salaries have been increased this year. The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. LaRiv-iere) has proved that to a demonstration. I was much amused that the member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley) should expect any modesty from the ministers of the present government. My remark may not apply to the Prime Minister and it may, but, it certainly is a fact that all the other ministers from first to last, are anxious to avail of every possible occasion to make a stump speech to their own glorification. The Postmaster General to-night has claimed great credit for the success of his department, but he has failed to show that he has inaugurated anything which would bring about that success. We know that this prosperity of the department is largely, if not entirely, due to the prosperity which has prevailed of recent years throughout Canada, and for that matter throughout the civilized world. He told us that the number of post offices had increased during the Liberal regime at the rate of 149 per annum, but if he looks back to 1891, or even to 1871, he will find that each year up to the coming into power of the Liberals, there was an increase of 149 in the number of post offices, and possibly more. I rose more particularly to bring to the attention of the House the case of the accounting postmasters. I had the opportunity of meeting the Postmaster General in company with the deputation of accounting postmasters who waited upon him, and I shall read the memorial which they presented, and which shows that the decrease in postage from three cents to two cents has been largely taken out of their income. In order that I may quote their case

properly, I propose to read their petition, so that it may be recorded on ' Hansard.'
It is on ' Hansard ' twice already.

Then I will put it on three
times, so that you will not have to hunt so far back for it. Let me say in the first place, that some years ago the matter of an increase in the remuneration to these postmasters, was urged by the member for Cardwell (Mr. Johnston). To-night we have the member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) making a display, and no doubt he was advised as to what was coming from the Postmaster General.
He was rehearsing.

Certainly, but it is to the member for Cardwell (Mr. Johnston) that the postmasters have to be thankful for pressing their claims upon the government. Here is the petition to which I refer :
Winnipeg, Manitoba, February, 1903. To the Right Hon. Sir William Mulook, Postmaster General,
Ottawa.
Sir,-We. the undersigned, accounting postmasters of Manitoba and the North-west Territories, beg to bring to your attention the following statement of facts regarding our work which goes to show that the remuneration is most inadequate, in the hope that you may be able to grant us substantial and immediate relief. We do this the more hopefully in view of the stand you have taken on the question of the hours of labour. &e., of the workingman.
1.	The postmaster is responsible for the safe handling of many important letters, and valuable parcels. In this country large amounts of money formerly sent by express are now sent by registered mail to wheat buyers to enable them to carry on their business. In many places the branch banks remit to, or receive from, the head office large sums of money. This increases the postmaster's responsibility and where help is employed necessitates care in the selection. The money-order business necessitates the handling of large sums of money for the miserable pittance of 25 cents per $100. The amount of stamps kept on hand must always be large with the source of supply so far away. In no other line of work would persons be held responsible for the proper handling of such large amounts, with the same possibilities of irregularities and losses, without remuneration at least from five to ten times greater than the postmaster receives for his money-order work. In many cases there is added responsibility through the handling of customs parcels for which there is practically no remuneration. The postmaster is expected to provide a roomy, centrally located office without any regard to the rental which that office would command if leased for other purposes. The necessity for the correct and prompt despatch of all mails regardless of hours of arrival and departure is in many instances a very grave responsibility. Understanding that the present basis of remuneration has been in vogue for a quarter of a century or more we would respectfully point out various increases in work which clearly show that, although it may have been sufficient then it is utterly inadequate now.

You see, they knew the Postmaster General was also Minister of Labour, and they thought they would appeal to him on that score.
Firstly. In connection with newspapers and periodicals we think it a conservative estimate to assume that a family will now receive an average of six to eight times as many periodicals as a family would be receiving twenty-live years ago.
'Secondly. The use of the mails as a means of distributing advertising matter is a practice of recent years entirely and the quantity handled is simply enormous and constantly increasing. These increases affect both local distribution and the sorting of matter for forwarding to outside offices.
Thirdly. The recent reduction in the rate of letter postage necessitates (in the matter of Canadian and United States postage) an increase of fully fifty per cent in the number of letters handled before an increase of revenue can accrue, or an increase of salary he hoped for. In the case of British, and some other lines of foreign postage, the increase in the number of letters1 must be 150 per cent before we have established a basis for any possible increase in salary. A working out of the figures in this connection will establish that the postmasters are bearing from thirty to forty per cent of the expenses of the reduction so appreciated by the' public. This appears to be an altogether undue proportion.
That proves what I have already said, that the reduction in the postal rate from three cents to two cents, has, to a very great extent, been borne by the postmasters, owing to the fact that a very large number of them are remunerated by way of commission.
The introduction of the postal note system has increased the amount of labour out of proportion to the revenue attached. This method of remitting small amounts (chiefly to the city offices) has largely curtailed the sale of stamps which were formerly used. At offices where customs parcels are handled and distributed by mail to smaller offices, stamps are usually sent In payment of duty and cash is remitted to port of entry, again curtailing the sale of stamps received from the department.
2.	An examination into the method of handing customs parcels and the remuneration (even where any is allowed) will reveal the fact that the work actually required to be performed, which is considerable, is practically unpaid for. This is one of (he points which we desire to bring to your attention, that unremunerative work of this sort Is being multiplied while the revenue of the office is being held down by reduced rates of postage.
3.	In a number of the offices, besides keeping the office open throughout the regulation hours, the postmasters are compelled to await the arrival of a late evening train and again in some instances have to get up at 5 or 6 o'clock in the morning to despatch a mail, thus imposing unduly long hours of service without any allowance for any class of assistance, to say nothing of a competent assistant. In some offices, owing to the arivai of several different mails the public is entitled to call and demand individual attention several times during the day, whereas the basis of remuneration makes no special provision for this. In places where tri-weekly

trains carry the mails, the postmaster is compelled to remain eleven hours a day for six days a week and provide (if he would give the public anything approaching satisfactory service) for a portion of three days a week, one or more duly qualified assistants. His allowance is inadequate for his own support at present cost of living, thus providing nothing for the payment ,of assistants.
4.	In view of the amount of mail matter to be re-sorted and forwarded the forwarding allowances do not begin to pay for the work done or the extra office room required. Another department with a deficit.
5.	The allowance for rent, fuel, and light is decidedly inadequate. In practically every town where the post office is kept in a separate compartment, the room occupied could be leased for a rental in excess of the full allowance for rent, for heating and for lighting. In the town of Morris, the postmaster is allowed $100 for rent, fuel and light. For less space in the same building he receives from the Merchants Bank, $350 a year for rent, alone. At Melita the postmaster cancelled a lease bringing him a net annual rental of $180 to use the building Impost office purposes on an allowance of $125 for rent, fuel and light. Other similar examples could be cited. Fuel and light are costly here.
6.	In the matter of securing proper assistants, we could point out that labour readily commands far larger remuneration in any market than it did a few years ago. To have experienced help available is a severe drain upon the limited exchequer of the post-master who is unfortunate enough to require it as nearly all do. Even where help is not regularly required, competent assistance must be had if the postmaster is ever to seek recreation or relief from duty.
7.	There is another matter which affects- postmasters in the west more particularly, namely, the increased cost of living. This has frequently been brought to the attention of yourself and colleagues in various ways, and we note that already you have conceded the point as in the case of the 20 per cent increase allowed the letter-carriers of Winnipeg.
And I see that they get a greater increase by tips new Act and the $50,000 which is voted in these estimates for the outside service.
In our opinion this does not represent the actual amount of difference, but is a recognition of that difference. In all lines the cost of living has advanced during the past few years, while the postmasters are receiving less pay for more work.
8.	A comparison with salaries paid in other departments of the public service and even in other departments of the postal service give an idea of our disadvantages. For example. First class railway mail clerks receive $960 and mileage, second-class clerks, $800 and mileage. In the city of Winnipeg the assistant postmaster gets $2,000, first-class clerks, $1,500, second-class, $1,320, third-class, $880, and letter-carriers. $720. We do not think these are too highly paid, but an office with a revenue of $2,000 not only absorbs all of one person's time, but requires an additional clerk at least a portion of the year. The postmaster of such an office receives for salary, commissions and allowances an average of less than $700 or less than half the amount received by a first-class city clerk, $100 less than a second-class railway mail clerk, and a trills less than is. paid -to. the city letter-carriers, and out of this modest income he must employ whatever additional help is required and furnish a
suitable office and office equipment. In most cases his hours are longer and his responsibilities greater than those of any of the officials referred to. In one town where the train arrived late and departed early, the postmaster until recently received $3.50 per month for overtime, while the railway agent received $19 a month extra.	[DOT]
In view of the conditions and facts set forth above, we would respectfully suggest the following changes as tending to bring about a redress of our grievances. 1st. That the straight salary allowance be based on 50 per cent on the first $1,000 worth of stamps sold, and 40 per cent on all additional sales. This would barely offset the loss resulting from the reduction of letter postage.
As I said before, these gentlemen understand how to properly make this calculation; and, instead of meeting that request, the Postmaster General gives them an increase of only ten per cent.
2nd. That in Manitoba a special increase of at least 20 per cent be allowed to cover extra cost of living. 3rd. That the allowance for rent, fuel and light be doubled so as to provide a reasonable rent for the office, and a provision for the cost of fuel and lignt in this country. 4th. That the -money order system be simplified so as to lessen the amount of work performed for the small remuneration allowed and also to increase its popularity with the business public, who now object to the restrictions hedging it round. 5th. in addition to the regular and general scale of allowances we would request. That a special allowance be granted for each extra mail which tends to bring the public again before the wicket for individual attention during the day. That the forward allowance be materially increased to distributing offices. That a special allowance be given to postmasters who are compelled to work before 8 a.m., or after 7 p.m. Among the mechanical Industries the special allowance for overtime is very marked. That in the case of offices where mails are so infrequent as to have large quantities of mail matter delivered at the office at one time, so that the public convenience really requires the employment of one or more assistants, an allowance be given towards the payment of such assistant or assistants.
I may say that in our western towns the express company to a very great extent is cutting into the business of the money-order office, almost doing the entire business, for the reason that a man can go to the express office, get his receipt a-nd do the business in one-half the time that it takes the postmaster to accomplish the same business; and I think it is as cheap or possibly cheaper. This is a matter in which I hope the Postmaster General, when he next addresses the House, will be able to show that he has done something to better the system.
6th. In addition to the above we feel that there are a number of cases of special, minor grievances which we cannot enter into in detail, but in which we think that a little investigation would show that redress could be effected so as to relieve the postmasters concerned without in any way iraparing the efficiency and safety of the public service, which grievances have probably continued to exist because they have not been brought to your honourable attention.

Now, they have been brought and placed on ' Hansard,' and the .Postmaster General will have them before him, and the members of this House can refer to them.
And we would respectfully urge that the above matters be duly considered and that a large measure of redress be granted In the very near future.
And your petitioners as in duty bound will ever pray.
Here is another small paragraph :
Supplementary Suggestions Passed by Executive.
1.	That all accounting offices be given an allowance for rent, fuel and light.
2.	That twine, mucilage, pens, ink, pencils, &c., for post office use be furnished by the department and not at the expense of the postmaster as at present.
S. That the department make it more clear to all publishers that newspapers must be suitably folded and that they must be addressed plainly. That where labels are used they must be in large clear type, and that if possible uniformity of colour in labels be secured.
4.	That a full list of ' Suggestions to the Public ' be printed by the department and supplied to all postmasters for display in their offices as tending to make it clear that certain regulations are found necessary by the department and are not based on the caprice or convenience of the postmaster. For instance that stamps an 1 moneys orders may not be purchased during the distribution of a newly arrived mail, and that money orders and postal notes are not available for purchase after the registered mail closes for an outgoing mail. Also some suggestions as to the age of children who are to be considered as proper persons to receive mail from the wicket.
5.	That when instructions are sent out for the weighing of all mails that facilities for such weighing be afforded by the department.
6.	That in view of the large sums of money at times in the mails in this country and hence often stored in the post office, and in view of the value of the stamps and the importance of the books now to be kept that safes be provided for accounting postmasters or an allowance be granted to pay for use of same when provided by the postmaster.
Now, I think these are very important suggestions which have been made by these accounting postmasters, and they should receive the close attention of the Postmaster General and his assistants. The hon. gentleman referred in his speech to the prosperity which has attended the department; but at ihe same time he failed to show us by what policy or by what changes, he has caused this improvement in the working of the department. Here even the postmasters make a number of practical suggestions to him which he might have thought of or acted upon. He gives $80,000 to officials, many of whom are well paid to-day, many of whom would not be able to earn the same amount of money in any other capacity in life many of whom thrown on their own resources would scarcely earn one-half of what they are getting; and yet these postmasters, the men who are bearing a great part of the burden and who have brought about this prosperity, are paid the Mr. BOYD.
small pittance of ten per cent. The hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) says that that matter has been on ' Hansard ' before. Well, if it has, why was not something done before ? It was not because the hon. minister did not know that the country was prosperous. He could have satisfied those people and saved them the expense of coming here to lay their case before the House and demand redress. I think that I am within my rights in bringing to the attention of the hon. minister this matter, which he has failed to meet, although he has looked after a class which has not done anything to bring about the prosperity of his department. The men he has overlooked are the men who have brought about that increase, and they should have the support of the hon. minister, but instead, these other men, many of whom .are now receiving more than they could in any other capacity, are looked after to the tune of $80,000.

I am sure that the Committee listened with much attention to the statement of the Postmaster General. It is quite evident that the whole thing was very well arranged. As an hon. gentleman has said, there was a little rehearsal to-night, and an opportunity given the hon. minister of making the statement be did. He said that there are $292,000 to the credit of the Post Office Department after paying the whole service. That is not a difficult matter. If the hon. gentleman has additional receipts it is because he has increased the burdens of the people. True, there has been a decrease in the postage on letters, but there has been ah increase on other mail matter, and therefore it is not difficult to see how the hon. gentleman, for the first time since he has been in office, has been able to show a surplus of $292,000. What is the history of the department during the six preceding years from 1897 to 1902 ? The hon. gentleman had a deficit every year during that period and a total deficit of $2,991,896.
It will take some time to pay that up.

Yes, the hon. gentleman has starved the service. He is not giving the supply of post offices to the rural districts and elsewhere which they should have had. Let me prove this. The number of post offices that were opened between 1890 and 1896, for a period of six years under Conservative rule, was 1.190. That was a period of great depression, but take this period of phenomenal expansion from 1896 to 1902, under the administration of the hon. gentleman, and we find that instead of the post offices being increased 1,190, the increase is only 855. Could you find more conclusive evidence that the hon. gentleman has increased the burdens of the people and starved the service at the same

time ? Under such conditions, it is not difficult for the bon. gentleman to have a surplus. What was the cost per head in 189G for the postal service ? It was 93 cents, and in 1902 the cost was 90 cents per head. I need not pursue the case any further. That conclusively proves that the hon. gentleman has not kept up with our increased prosperity by giving rural districts the postal service to which they are entitled. While the postage was lowered on certain classes of mail matter, it has been, on the other hand, increased to such an extent that the cost per head to the people is larger in 1901 than it was in 1890. The hon. gentleman seeks to impress upon the people the idea that he has given Canada a better service, but the fact that the post offices have not been increased in the same ratio during his regime as they did during the previous regime disposes of that claim. It is clear that the hon. gentleman has not met the wants of the people, and that being the case, he has not very much to boast of. But what he has proved1 is that he has taken more money from the people and given them worse service.

There are certain things one would require to know before determining whether it is to the good management of the Post Office Department that we owe this increased revenue. I see in the hon. gentleman's report, at the end of page 4, appendix A, the statement that for the year ending June 30th, 1902, the net revenue of the Post Office Department was $3,888,126.10 being an increase over the revenue of the previous year of $466,933,91, or 13'64 per cent. The increase in expenditure was $45,040.78, equal to 1T9 per cent. There was evidently a process of starving going on there, because that increase of expenditure was not an increase commensurate with tiie development of the country. Evidently those who carried the mails and the postmasters were not paid very extravagantly for their work. There was an item last year, which I presume is the same this ' year, that is about the automobiles used in Toronto? Are they in use still?
Yes.
I understood last year that they were not charged to the Post Office Department?	.
They are now, but the change does not amount to anything.
They are taken into account in tlie statement. There are steamship subsidies for mail service, are these taken into account?
They are treated as they always were. 1 think most of our mails go to England by the United States. We have to pay the transit charges.

But we give large subsidies for mail service on the steamers. That is not, however, a matter of any great importance if treated in the same way as it was before. I see here, in the report which the Postmaster General has submitted to the House, that there was a surplus of revenue over expenditure up to 30th June, 1902 for the first time.
That was omitting the Yukon. There is a special reference to it in the report.

Yes, you have both omitted and put it in in this instance, and with the cost of the Yukon taken out, there is still a surplus of $292,702. I do not know whether I took down the hon. gentleman's statement correctly, but I understood him to say that in 1890 there was a deficit of $781,152. I think that was wiped out by an item put in the estimates.

The department, for the fiscal year ending 30fli June, 1896, had a deficit, as I have already explained, on the operations of that year, of $781,000. They failed to take a vote from parliament for that year sufficient to pay the working expenses ; and when I took office I found there were about three-quarters of a million dollars of unpaid accounts for the fiscal year ending 30th June, 1896, for which there was no parliamentary appropriation. I reported the matter to the Finance Minister, and in the succeeding year I took an item wherewith to pay these accounts.
Then after everything was paid you started afresh ?

It is the policy of the department to pay up everything each year, to have no arrears after the 30tli of June. Last year there was a slight error, that policy was not lived up to as it ought to have been, and there was an error through the department having failed to estimate the amount correctly. They were $22,000 short, and that amount had to be carried over in the report of that year, and in the fiscal year of 1903 we paid that shortage of the preceding year. Therefore, by that amount our showing is that much worse this year. But with that exception, the policy I have mentioned has been lived up to, and >ve close up the year's accounts and take a vote from parliament each year, so that there can be no accumulated deficit, as was the practice for many years in former times. I say in frankness that that practice prevailed under both Liberal and Conservative governments down to 1896.
Then there must have been a much larger deficit than $7S1,000, because there was an overlapping that was brought down.
It is true there were a lot of errors, and two

I wish to say that the policy of the Postmaster General in increasing the salaries of the postmasters throughout the country is in my judgment in the right direction. The only complaint that I have to make is that he has not gone far enough. We are not now troubled so much in hunting up postmasters since the present government came into power, lie-cause they generally leave that responsibility upon others. But I do know that I have been obliged to hunt up postmasters many times, and it was difficult to get them to take the position at all for a salary ranging from $12 to $25. As they used to say, it did not pay them for scrubbing the floor. I said at one time that the minimum salary should be $25. I think now it should be higher, I do not think any one should be expected to keep a post office for less than $35 a year. What principle does the Postmaster General follow now in striking salaries above that ? I understood him to say that they get 10 per cent more than they got before.
They are paid on the same scale, but we add on 10 per cent.
Since there is a surplus now, 1 would suggest to make that increase about 20 per cent.
The hon. gentleman would land me in a deficit at once. The various increases already provided for are very near the surplus I have spoken of.
When the hon. gentleman reduced the postage on letters, what effect did it have on the pay of the postmasters throughout the country ?

No postmaster had his salary reduced, because of the reduction in the rate. The salaries were allowed to remain at the rate at which they stood before the reduction. Preceding governments had reduced the rate without regard to the compensation of the postmasters. Many in this House will remember when the letter postage was five cents, perhaps more than that. But the commissions were left the same.
I still think that a great many rural postmasters are underpaid. Take the case of the postmaster in my own township of Edville. There is a daily .

mail, for it is a populous section of country. It is five or six miles from the villages of Colborne and Brighton. He is attentive to his duty, the office is kept open from morning till night, and the postmaster only gets $30. If he had not his daughter there to attend to the post office he could not keep it open. I have heard it stated here to-night that men often keep a post office to draw custom. Well, they must have a store for that purpose. But there are many post offices in our section that have no store in connection with them. I think these gentlemen should be paid something more. I am not an advocate of extravagance, but i am favourable to a reasonable expenditure where it is necessary to pay men for attending to an office like that. I am satisfied that the amount hardly pays that man. I am at the office frequently, and I am satisfied that the amount of money will hardly pay for the wood that is consumed in keeping the place warm. I think these are men who are underpaid. They are doing what is very beneficial to the rural districts. It is a great pleasure for men living in the rural districts to realize that they can get their mail and know that they are not circumscribed as to hours, but that they can get it any time in the day.

When the hon. minister was devising ways and means to make his revenue and expenditure he changed the system which before that time allowed all papers and parliamentary documents of the legislative assembly to go through the post office free.
No, there has been no change.

I am quite sure that I am not in error. I have evidence of it in my hand. Here is a letter from a clerk of the peace.
Gffice of the Clerk of the Peace for Leeds and Grenville,
Brockville, September 14, 1903.
Dear 'Sir,-I beg to inform you that I have received the Ontario Statutes, for 1903, for distribution. If you wish them sent to you by book post send me 33 cents in postage stamps to prepay postage and sign and return me the enclosed receipt.
(Sgd.) M. M. BROWN,
Clerk of the Peace.

There never was a time in the history of the country when provision was made by which clerks of the peace could transmit papers through the post office free. The Post Office Act says what may and what may not be mailed free. The Post Office Act says what local parliamentary papers may go free. The Act that was in force when we took office is in force to-day. There has been no change whatever in the application of the Act. Whatever went free then goes free to-day.
I am quite sure that there was a time, whether it was in the time of the Postmaster General or not, when these books went free. I am sure there was a change made. I remember it distinctly.

If every official of the local government, or if clerks of the peace all over Canada, could frank matter where would be the end of the franking privilege ? It.may be that in days gone by such a practice prevailed but it has not for many years or long before we came into office. The hon. gentleman surely would not urge a policy of that kind.

I am talking quite properly in connection with my rights. I am not urging the policy of that kind but I am drawing attention to a complaint that is made. I am not prepared to say that the fault, if fault there is, lies with the hon. Postmaster General or that there was free delivery of this matter before through the post office. But I know that my impression is that other papers used to go through the post office free which do not now.
There was no cutting off

The hon. Postmaster General may say that there was no cutting off but my memory is just as good as his and I make the statement that there was a cutting off. I have a distinct remembrance of having a controversy with the postmaster in our own locality in regard to what he should allow to go through the mails free and I know that in that case there was a cutting off.
Not by me. If such a state of affairs existed in days gone by I know nothing about it. There has been no change in that respect under my administration.

I was about to say that in many of these lines the additional postage put on, such as for instance, the additional postage put on newspapers has helped to give the additional revenue that we have to-day, and I have no doubt a great deal was made up from the increased correspondence carried on on account of the larger amount of business done. For everything that the hon. Postmaster General has done he is entitled to credit, but I do not know whether it is in order to throw as many bouquets as the hon. member for King's, Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hughes) desires to present to him because that hon. gentleman desires to give him credit for a great deal of what he did not accomplish as well as for a great deal that he did accomplish. For anything that he has accomplished he is entitled to credit. He is entitled to credit for increasing the number of post offices which I think is a step in the right direction. He has also increased the mail service. That,
I think, is in the right direction as well, but I think there has not been that expansion that there should have been in the pay of the mail contractors and of the small postmasters throughout the country. I think the postmasters in the towns and cities did not fare so badly, but in the small villages throughout the country where postmasters are obliged to keep the offices for anywhere from $25 to $35 there is room for improvement.

I must congratulate the hon. Postmaster General upon the generous heart he has shown towards the country postmasters in giving them an increase in their salaries. The amounts they have been receiving in the past have been very inadequate for the services they have rendered. I know several postmasters that I have had a great deal of difficulty in persuading to remain in office because of the small pittance they have been receiving, amounting to $12 a year. I am very glad to know that their salaries are now being increased. They are deserving of that increase and I would have liked if it had been still larger. I would like also if the hon. Postmaster General could see his way clear with the revenue that is now afforded to his department to allow newspapers to be distributed free. This is literature that should pass free as its distribution is advancing the knowledge of the country not only in political but in other matters. Whilst I am on my feet I may say that uje have a post office on the Cornwall road at New Cornwall, with John E. Hallimore as postmaster. An application on behalf of the people in that district has been made for a tri-weekly instead of a weekly service. It is a very thickly settled district and one that is deserving of a more frequent mail service. I believe that the hon. Postmaster General, from what he said when I had an interview with him the other day, will make an arrangement to give a tri-weeldy service to this parish from Mahone Bay. We have a railway passing through my county and I can see no reason why the mail could not be dropped at the different places along the line once a day instead of weekly. There is one office that is only receiving a weekly mail although the train passes by daily. Very often letters are delayed either in transit to or from the various points for want of a daily mail.
What is the name of the place to which the hon. gentleman refers ?

Block House, between Mahone Bay and Bridgewater, on the main line. If a tri-weekly mail is granted to New Cornwell from Mahone Bay that office can be served tri-weekly by the courier that would serve the office at New Cornwall. This is a reasonable request and I feel satisfied that the hon. Postmaster General

will see it in tlie same light and give it favourable consideration.

In looking over the report of the hon. Postmaster General, I see that the deficit for the first year of the hon. gentleman's administration ending the 30th June, 1897, was $586,540; in 1898, a deficit of $47,602 ; in 1899, a deficit of $457,420 ; in 1900, a deficit of $553,242 ; in 1901, a deficit of $512,014 ; in 1902, a deficit of $82,376. In these six years there was a total deficit of $2,239,194. The Postmaster General claims a surplus for the year ending June, 1903, of $292,702, so that this would leave a total deficit during the hon. gentleman's administration of $1,946,492. May I ask if that includes in each and every year the figures of the deficit with reference to the Yukon ?

We commenced the Yukon mail service in 1897, I think, but of course it has developed very much since. In each annual report since we established the Yukon service, the hon. gentleman will find a special reference to that service. It has been the policy of the department up to the present to show separately the revenue and expenditure on the Yukon service, apart from the general service for the rest of Canada.
Will the minister state the deficit in the Yukon postal service from its establishment up to the present ?
I cannot give you that to-night.
What increase does the minister purpose to give to the town postmasters, and how will he distinguish between the town and the village postmasters ?
There is no distinction between town and village. All postmasters who are paid by commission will now receive an increase of 10 per cent over what they were receiving before.

I congratulate the Postmaster General upon realizing his ambition of having a surplus. I trust it will not become a fad with him to go on increasing these surpluses until he wipes out the deficits that have accumulated under his administration of seven years. If he attempted such a thing the post office service would be starved to death. I congratulate the Postmaster General on the prosperity of the country which has made it possible for him to realize that surplus. I have been spending a fewT weeks in the sparsely settled districts of the North-west, where the people are coming in so rapidly, and where for distances of over sixty and seventy miles which I have travelled, they have no mail service. I can quite understand that when the Postmaster General thought of the expense of carrying the mails into these out-Mr. KAULBACH.
lyiug territories, and wishing to have a surplus, he would not venture to give them an adequate mail service. I would impress upon the Postmaster General, the absolute necessity of dispelling from his mind any idea of making the Post Office Department pay in the immediate future, seeing that we have so much development of that service before us. Those who have been used to living in closely settled communities iu Europe or eastern Canada, find it very lonely when they settle on the western plains. Railway development has been very slow in that territory of recent years, and settlement is going long distances away from any centre of communication. The settlers are naturally desirous of being able to communicate with their people at home, and nothing stimulates immigration so much as the giving of facilities for that purpose. Any one who visits these communities and sees the anxiety with which the people await the coming of the mail, will appreciate that fact. In the district I refer to, there were only three settlers three years ago, but now there are more than fifty families. The mail is carried in by any one who happens to be able to take it by accident, and it is tumbled about from one house to another until a store is established, when that is made the central point of distribution. The Postmaster General must see how unsatisfactory such a system is. Let me say, that while I am perfectly satisfied that the Postmaster General should increase the salaries of country postmasters, I do' not know that I am so very much wrapt up in that idea, as other hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, perhaps I am not so much dependent upon them. While I have no objection to the Postmaster General increasing the salaries of these gentlemen, yet I certainly would not desire that his doing so should lead to the starvation of the mail service in western Canada, because I look upon the development of the mail service in the west as being absolutely essential to the satisfactory settlement of that country. Believing as I do, that the development of the west is more important to us than the increasing of the salaries of country postmasters, so far as I am personally concerned, I hope that the Postmaster General will see that whatever increases in salaries he makes, they will not be taken from the mail service of the west. I trust that in the future the Postmaster General will not let a few hundred dollars expense interfere with the development of our postal service.

I quite appreciate the importance of giving to the people who are coming into our North-west, the best possible mail service. When an application is made for a post office that application is referred to the inspector and he makes a report. I think I am strictly within the facts when I say, that in no instance has there been any refusal to estab-

lish a post office which has been recommended by the inspector. Indeed, in many instances I have established post offices where the inspector recommended they were not necessary. If the inspector recommends it, the office is established, and it may be relied upon that Mr. McLeod, the inspector in that territory, a capable and intelligent man will make recommendations wherever there is reasonable justification. I think no one can complain that we have not liberally extended the post offices throughout the territories.
To provide fbr an appointment oi. seven additional railway mail clerks-$3,500.
What is this for ?

In Manitoba and the North-west Territories.
Telegraph lines, Yukon system-working expanses, $62,000.
The MINISTER OI<' PUBLIC WORKS. This is for the maintenance and operation of these lines.
What is the experience of the working of these lines ?
The operation costs $179,000 in rbund numbers, and the receipts this year, judging by the nine months, will amount to about $120,000, leaving a deficit of a little over $50,000.
Is the deficit growing smaller or larger every year ?

The construction account was closed only a few months ago. The revenue is increasing. Last month it was $14,000, which is a couple of thousand dollars larger than ever before. The rates had been perhaps prematurely lowered. The expenses can be cut down after this year, I think, to some extent, so that I imagine the deficit will decrease every year.
What does the minister mean by the rates being prematurely lowered ? Last year the Minister of Public Works promised to test the question of lowering the rates.
They were lowered some months ago from $4.50, I think, to $3 for ten words, and the press rate has been reduced from 3 cents a word to 4 cent a word.
What means has the minister for repairing the lines ?
There are linemen at stations along the lines. This expense increases the cost of operating these lines beyond the ordinary lines.	.

I understand that the increase of revenue has come about since the reduction in rates ?
The MINISTER OB' PUBLIC WORKS. Of course, the line was not completed. The large branches which have been added to the line contribute to the deficit, as they do not yield much revenue.

Where do these branches run ?
The MINISTER OB' PUBLIC WORKS. The longest runs to Port Simpson. The prospect is that the revenue will improve and the expenditure will decrease.
Can the minister give us the figures of the total construction account to date ?
It is a little less than $900,000.

Can he give us the amount paid on construction account during this year ?
The MINISTER OB' PUBLIC WORKS.
I cannot tell my hon. friend. The construction account is now closed.

subtopic: MESSAGE FROM THE GOVERNOR GENERAL-FURTHER SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES.

speechtext:
The MINISTER OF FINANCE presented a message from His Excellency the Governor General.
Mr. SPEAKER read the message as follows :
Minto.
The Governor General transmits to the House of Commons Further Supplementary Estimates of sums required for the service of the Dominion for the year ending 30th June, 1904, and in accordance with the provisions of ' The British North America Act, 1867,' the Governor General recommends these Estimates to the House of Commons.
Government House,
Ottawa, 14th October, 1903.
On motion of the Minister of Finance, the Message and Supplementary Estimates were referred to the Committee of Supply.
The MINISTER 'OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.
